# #30DayMapChallenge, Submission Day 10

&gt; &quot;Prompting only&quot; - For this map, make AI work for its money and produce something
from start to finish in a chat window or on the command line.

We are going to be working towards building a submission for this day. The
idea is to create a map of the areas in the UK with the most dissimilar
neighboring LSOAs. We will measure similarity with AlphaEarth embeddings, and
areas with official LSOA polygons. 

## Data

We are going to be working with Imago&#x27;s embeddings product:

&gt; https://data.imago.ac.uk/datasets/google-satellite-embedding-v1-small-areas-2017-2024

We will start playing with 2024, but we might explore looking at change later
on.

## Similarity

In this context, we will describe similarity of two LSOAs as the distance 
between their two embedding vectors.

We might also explore a variation where we compute similarity between a given
LSOA and _all_ of its surrounding neighbors.

## Tools

We will, at least, rely on geopandas for working with the data, and PySAL for
working with topology/contiguity. Please examine the documentation for the
migration to the new `Graph` structure for spatial weights:

&gt; https://pysal.org/libpysal/stable/user-guide/graph/w_g_migration.html

## Reading data

Imago ships one GeoPackage per year, each holding small-area polygons (British National Grid, EPSG:27700) alongside the mean of each of the 64 embedding bands within the area. We start with 2024 and split the attributes into an embedding matrix for later distance calculations.
@@code
YEAR = 2024
lsoas = gpd.read_file(f&quot;data/extracted-lsoa-geopackage_{YEAR}_output.gpkg&quot;)

print(lsoas.crs, lsoas.shape)
lsoas.index.str[0].value_counts().rename({&quot;E&quot;: &quot;England&quot;, &quot;W&quot;: &quot;Wales&quot;, &quot;S&quot;: &quot;Scotland&quot;, &quot;N&quot;: &quot;N. Ireland&quot;})
@@code
emb = lsoas[band_cols].to_numpy()
norms = np.linalg.norm(emb, axis=1)
print(&quot;NaN rows:&quot;, np.isnan(emb).any(axis=1).sum())
pd.Series(norms).describe()
EOF

::: {.reply}
I've read the spec, created `gdsl30dmc.ipynb` with a **Setup** section and a **Reading data** section, and run it. Everything executes without errors.

**What's in the 2024 data:**

- **46,844 small areas covering the whole UK:** 33,755 in England, 7,392 in Scotland, 3,780 in Northern Ireland and 1,917 in Wales. Scotland's areas are Data Zones and Northern Ireland's are Super Data Zones, not LSOAs, so "LSOA" here really means the small-area unit used in each nation.

- **Columns:** the `data_zone_code` ID, 64 columns `band1_mean`…`band64_mean`, and the polygons, already in British National Grid. No values are missing.

- **The vectors aren't unit length:** their lengths range from 0.75 to 0.99. AlphaEarth gives every pixel a unit-length vector, so averaging them over an area shrinks the result, and it shrinks more the more mixed the area's land cover is. That bears on how we measure distance, below.

- **Harmless warning:** the read cell prints a PROJ "Open of …/share/proj failed" error. The CRS still resolves correctly (`EPSG:27700`), so you can ignore it.

**Decisions before the contiguity and similarity section:**

1. **Coverage:** keep all four nations, or only Great Britain? Northern Ireland doesn't touch the rest, so it would be its own block of neighbours either way.

2. **Contiguity:** I'd use queen, where areas sharing a corner count as neighbours, via `graph.Graph.build_contiguity(lsoas, rook=False)`. Islands with no neighbours, such as Scilly and parts of the Hebrides, would be flagged and dropped.

3. **Distance:** I'd use Euclidean distance, as SPEC.md says. Cosine distance is the alternative: it compares only the direction of the vectors, so it ignores the shrinkage from mixed land cover. I'd add it as a quick comparison.

4. **How to map it:** the first map could colour each area by the mean distance to its neighbours, which is the "all surrounding neighbours" idea in SPEC.md. The alternative is to draw the shared boundaries themselves, coloured by how different the two areas on each side are. The boundary version is more literal and probably makes the more striking map.

My suggestion for the next section is **Building the contiguity graph**, followed by **Neighbour dissimilarity**. Tell me your picks, or say "go" and I'll proceed with all four nations, queen contiguity, Euclidean distance, and both the boundary map and the per-area map.

build_contiguity(geometry, rook=True, by_perimeter=False, strict=False) class method of libpysal.graph.base.Graph
    Generate Graph from geometry based on contiguity

    Contiguity builder assumes that all geometries are forming a coverage, i.e.
    a non-overlapping mesh and neighbouring geometries share only points or
    segments of their exterior boundaries. In practice, ``build_contiguity`` is
    capable of creating a Graph of partially overlapping geometries when
    ``strict=False, by_perimeter=False``, but that would not strictly follow the
    definition of queen or rook contiguity.

    Parameters

        shapely.Geometry objects is passed, Graph will assume a RangeIndex.

        Contiguity method. If True, two geometries are considered neighbours if
        they share at least one edge. If False, two geometries are considered
        neighbours if they share at least one vertex. By default True
    by_perimeter : bool, optional
        If True, ``weight`` represents the length of the shared boundary between
        adjacent units, by default False. For row-standardized version of perimeter
        weights, use
        ``Graph.build_contiguity(gdf, by_perimeter=True).transform(&quot;r&quot;)``.
    strict : bool, optional
        Use the strict topological method. If False, the contiguity is determined
        based on shared coordinates or coordinate sequences representing edges.
        This assumes geometry coverage that is topologically correct. This method
        is faster but can miss some relations. If True, the contiguity is
        determined based on geometric relations that do not require precise
        topology. This method is slower but will result in correct contiguity
        even if the topology of geometries is not optimal. By default False.

        libpysal.graph.Graph encoding contiguity weights

build_fuzzy_contiguity(geometry, tolerance=None, buffer=None, predicate=&#x27;intersects&#x27;, **kwargs) class method of libpysal.graph.base.Graph
    Generate Graph from fuzzy contiguity

    Fuzzy contiguity relaxes the notion of contiguity neighbors
    for the case of geometry collections that violate the condition
    of planar enforcement. It handles three types of conditions present
    in such collections that would result in missing links when using
    the regular contiguity methods.

    The first are edges for nearby polygons that should be shared, but are
    digitized separately for the individual polygons and the resulting edges
    do not coincide, but instead the edges intersect. This case can also be
    covered by ``build_contiguty`` with the ``strict=False`` parameter.

    The second case is similar to the first, only the resultant edges do not
    intersect but are &quot;close&quot;. The optional buffering of geometry then closes the
    gaps between the polygons and a resulting intersection is encoded as a link.

    The final case arises when one polygon is &quot;inside&quot; a second polygon but is not
    encoded to represent a hole in the containing polygon.

    It is also possible to create a contiguity based on a custom spatial predicate.

    Parameters

    tolerance : float, optional
        The percentage of the length of the minimum side of the bounding rectangle
        for the ``geoms`` to use in determining the buffering distance. Either
        ``tolerance`` or ``buffer`` may be specified but not both.
        By default None.
    buffer : float, optional
        Exact buffering distance in the units of ``geoms.crs``. Either
        ``tolerance`` or ``buffer`` may be specified but not both.
        By default None.

## Building the contiguity graph

We connect areas that share at least one boundary point (queen contiguity) using the new `libpysal.graph.Graph` API, keeping all four nations. Since the polygons come from four national statistical agencies, we first try the standard builder and check how many links cross national borders, where boundaries may not line up.
EOF

%%time
g_queen = graph.Graph.build_contiguity(lsoas, rook=False)
g_queen.summary()
EOF
nb cell update gdsl30dmc.ipynb -c cdc3ef18-37c4-482b-9ade-dfc73b2a562c --source - &lt;&lt;&#x27;EOF&#x27;
nation = pd.Series(lsoas.index.str[0], index=lsoas.index)

def link_types(g):
    &quot;&quot;&quot;Count directed links by nation pair, ignoring isolates&#x27; zero-weight self-loops.&quot;&quot;&quot;
    adj = g.adjacency.reset_index()
    adj = adj[adj.focal != adj.neighbor]
    return pd.Series(nation.loc[adj.focal].values + &quot;-&quot; + nation.loc[adj.neighbor].values).value_counts()

link_types(g_queen)
EOF
nb cell add gdsl30dmc.ipynb -a cdc3ef18-37c4-482b-9ade-dfc73b2a562c --source - &lt;&lt;&#x27;EOF&#x27;
@@markdown
### Fixing the England–Scotland border

Only one England–Scotland pair is linked, even though about two dozen pairs of areas meet along that border. The two nations&#x27; polygons slightly *overlap* there (by up to ~70,000 m²), and contiguity only counts polygons that touch without overlapping. Fuzzy contiguity links any pair of geometries that intersect, which covers touching (queen) and overlapping polygons alike, so it fixes the border without adding spurious links elsewhere.
@@code
%%time
g = graph.Graph.build_fuzzy_contiguity(lsoas)

edges = lambda g: set(g.adjacency[g.adjacency &gt; 0].index)
print(&quot;Links only in queen:&quot;, len(edges(g_queen) - edges(g)), &quot;| only in fuzzy:&quot;, len(edges(g) - edges(g_queen)))
link_types(g)
EOF

print(&quot;Isolates:&quot;, len(g.isolates), &quot;| Components:&quot;, g.n_components)
print(pd.Series(g.component_labels).value_counts().head(5))
g.cardinalities.describe()
EOF

::: {.reply}
I've built the contiguity graph for all four nations and run the notebook start to finish without errors. I've stopped there, before any similarity work.

**The problem:** the standard queen builder (`Graph.build_contiguity(..., rook=False)`) linked only **one** pair of areas across the England–Scotland border. About two dozen pairs actually meet there. The two nations' polygons overlap slightly along the border, by up to about 70,000 m² for a single pair, and contiguity only counts polygons that touch without overlapping. Wales–England was fine.

**The fix:** I used `Graph.build_fuzzy_contiguity(lsoas)` instead, which links any two polygons that intersect. It keeps every link the queen graph found, adds only the 21 missing England–Scotland pairs (23 in total now), and takes about 3 seconds instead of 18. It is now the main graph, `g`. The queen graph stays in the notebook as `g_queen` so the comparison is visible.

The final graph:

| | |

|---|---|

| Areas | 46,844 |

| Links between neighbouring areas | 272,466 (counted in both directions) |

| Neighbours per area | median 6, maximum 53 |

| Areas with no neighbours | 12 |

| Disconnected pieces | 31: mainland GB (42,777 areas), Northern Ireland (3,779), plus island groups (largest 89 areas) |

The 12 areas with no neighbours will need to be dropped or handled separately before we compute similarity.

The notebook now has a **Building the contiguity graph** section, with a subsection, **Fixing the England–Scotland border**, that shows the problem and the fix.

## 2026-11-04 — Contiguity graph (all four nations, queen)

**Data (2024):** 46,844 small areas — England 33,755 LSOAs, Scotland 7,392
Data Zones, Northern Ireland 3,780 Super Data Zones, Wales 1,917 LSOAs. EPSG:27700,
64 embedding bands (`band{1..64}_mean`), no missing values. Embedding vector
lengths are 0.75–0.99 rather than 1, because they are averages of unit-length pixel vectors.

**Queen contiguity** (`Graph.build_contiguity(lsoas, rook=False)`, ~18 s):
272,424 links (counted in both directions), but only **1** England–Scotland pair. Wales–England looked fine
(99 links each way). `strict=True` was worse: zero England–Scotland links, and 326 fewer
within Northern Ireland.

**Diagnosis:** polygons within 1 m of each other show ~23 England–Scotland pairs, all at
distance 0, which *overlap* by up to ~70,000 m² (the two nations&#x27; boundaries come from different sources).
Contiguity requires polygons to touch without overlapping, so these links are dropped.

**Fix:** `Graph.build_fuzzy_contiguity(lsoas)`, which links any polygons that intersect (~3 s). It contains every queen
link plus the 21 missing England–Scotland pairs (23 in total), and nothing else changed.

**Final graph `g`:** 272,466 links, median 6 neighbours per area (max 53), **12 areas with no neighbours**,
31 disconnected pieces (mainland GB 42,777; Northern Ireland 3,779; island groups, largest 89).
The areas with no neighbours need handling before we compute dissimilarity.</pre><pre class="tool-out">File created successfully at: LOG.md (file state is current in your context — no need to Read it back)</pre></details></details>
```

```{=html}
<div class="note prompt" id="p-10"><div class="note-meta"><a href="#p-10">#10</a> · Wed 4 Nov, 12:20</div><div class="note-text">cosine perhaps?</div></div>

::: {.reply}
Yes, I'd use cosine distance (1 − cosine similarity) as the main measure.

**Why cosine fits these vectors:**

- **It's how AlphaEarth embeddings are meant to be compared.** Each pixel's vector has length 1, and Google's guidance is to compare them with the dot product, which for unit-length vectors is the same as cosine similarity.

- **Averaging muddles the vector lengths.** Our area vectors are averages of pixel vectors, so their lengths (0.75–0.99) partly reflect how mixed an area's land cover is. Cosine ignores length and compares only direction, which here means the overall land-cover mix. Euclidean distance would also count a difference in mixedness: a uniform field next to a patchwork of fields with the same overall mix would look different.

- **It's easy to read.** Values run from 0 (same direction) to 2 (opposite).

**How much it matters:** probably not much. If you rescale each vector to length 1 first, squared Euclidean distance becomes exactly 2 × cosine distance, so the two give the same ranking. On the raw averages they can only differ through vector length, and those lengths vary little (standard deviation 0.034).

**What I'd suggest:**

1. Compute cosine distance for every pair of neighbouring areas, stored on the graph so we can map shared borders later.

2. As a quick check, also compute raw Euclidean distance and report how closely the two rankings agree (Spearman correlation). If they agree, we keep cosine and note that the choice didn't matter much. If they don't, the areas where they differ are worth mapping.

3. Hold off on combining the pairs into a single score per area (mean or max over its neighbours) until you've seen the pair-level distribution.

Want me to go ahead with steps 1–2 in a new **Neighbour dissimilarity** section?
:::


```{=html}
<div class="note prompt" id="p-11"><div class="note-meta"><a href="#p-11">#11</a> · Wed 4 Nov, 12:21</div><div class="note-text">let&#x27;s stick to cosine here. Open up a new section and let&#x27;s calculate the cosine distance (sklearn?) between every polygon and all of its queen neighors. Use the Graph we&#x27;ve created for this. Also, I think there&#x27;s scope here to make it work in parallel and it&#x27;d be significantly faster, what do you think? don&#x27;t do anything until we&#x27;re clear on what</div></div>
```


::: {.reply}
I'd skip parallelism: a single vectorised NumPy step will finish in well under a second. Here's the plan.

**The calculation:**

1. Take the neighbour pairs from `g.adjacency`, which is indexed by `focal` and `neighbor`: 272,466 rows, with each pair of neighbours appearing once in each direction.

2. Look up both areas' 64-band vectors and compute cosine distance for every pair in one go with `sklearn.metrics.pairwise.paired_cosine_distances(emb[i], emb[j])`. That's about 17 million multiplications, which takes milliseconds. Doing it by hand (normalise each row to length 1, then 1 minus the row-wise dot product) gives the same result.

3. Keep the results on the graph: a new graph `g_dist`, built with the same links as `g` but with the cosine distance as each link's weight. That lets us use the Graph machinery later, for example to average over each area's neighbours, and it gives us the pairs needed to map shared borders.

**Why not parallelise:**

- The work is one vectorised operation over a 272k × 64 array. Starting worker processes and copying data to them would take longer than the calculation itself.

- NumPy already uses compiled code for this kind of array maths.

- The slow parts of this workflow are building the graph (about 3 s) and plotting, not the distances.

- The thing to avoid is sklearn's `cosine_distances(emb)`, which would compute all 46k × 46k pairs (about 17 GB). Avoiding that is about using the graph's pairs, not about running in parallel.

**Two details to agree on:**

- **Which neighbours:** strictly, `g` is fuzzy contiguity, i.e. queen plus the 21 England–Scotland pairs whose polygons overlap. I'll use `g` so the border isn't cut, and say so in the section text.

- **Duplicate pairs:** each pair's distance is computed twice, once in each direction. Keeping both makes per-area summaries easy, and computing them twice costs almost nothing.

The new section would be **Neighbour dissimilarity**, with a short explanation, the distance calculation, and a summary plus histogram of the 272k pair distances.

from joblib import Parallel, delayed

        t = time.perf_counter()
        p = np.concatenate(Parallel(n_jobs=nj, backend=backend)(delayed(run)(i[c], j[c]) for c in chunks))
        print(f&quot;{backend} n_jobs={nj}: {time.perf_counter()-t:.3f}s  same={np.allclose(p, s)}&quot;)
EOF

```{=html}
<div class="note prompt" id="p-13"><div class="note-meta"><a href="#p-13">#13</a> · Wed 4 Nov, 12:24</div><div class="note-text">What I&#x27;m thinking is split all of the polygons in 16 chunks, one per core in this machine, and then calculate the distances for those polygons and their neighbors in a separate worker and collect all the results afterwards.</div></div>
```


::: {.reply}
Your scheme is correct, and with threads it is a little faster. With separate processes it is slower than not parallelising at all.

**Is the split correct?** Yes. `g.adjacency` is sorted by focal polygon, so 16 groups of polygons are just 16 contiguous blocks of rows. Each worker computes distances for its polygons and their neighbours, and joining the results gives exactly the serial answer. The test confirmed this (`same=True`).

**Timings from the test,** with the real sizes (46,832 areas, 272,466 pairs, 64 bands) on random vectors:

| Approach | Time |

|---|---|

| Serial, `paired_cosine_distances` | 0.97 s |

| Separate processes (joblib `loky`), 4 / 8 workers | 1.6 / 2.2 s |

| Threads (joblib `threading`), 4 / 8 workers | 0.34 / 0.23 s |

- **Separate processes lose.** Each worker has to be started and sent its share of the data, which takes longer than the calculation itself. More workers made it slower, so 16 would be worse still.

- **Threads win slightly.** NumPy releases Python's global interpreter lock while it computes, so threads share the arrays without copying them, and 8 threads were about 4× faster than serial.

- **Absolute numbers are tiny.** The saving is under a second, out of a notebook run that spends about 20 s on reading the data and graph building and about 40 s on the tile-map figure.

**My recommendation:** keep it serial. It's a single readable line in the notebook and costs about 1 s. If you want the parallel version anyway, for example because you plan to scale up to all eight years or wider neighbourhoods, I'd do your 16-chunk split with joblib's `threading` backend. That costs a few extra lines and saves less than a second.

Serial, or 16 thread chunks?
:::


```{=html}
<div class="note prompt" id="p-14"><div class="note-meta"><a href="#p-14">#14</a> · Wed 4 Nov, 12:26</div><div class="note-text">Is the code much more complex for the chunks?</div></div>
```


::: {.reply}
No, it's about four extra lines. Both versions share the same setup:

```python
from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import paired_cosine_distances

adj = g.adjacency
pos = pd.Series(np.arange(len(lsoas)), index=lsoas.index)  # area code → row in emb
i = pos.loc[adj.index.get_level_values("focal")].to_numpy()
j = pos.loc[adj.index.get_level_values("neighbor")].to_numpy()
```

**Serial:**

```python
dist = paired_cosine_distances(emb[i], emb[j])
```

**16 chunks with threads:**

```python
from joblib import Parallel, delayed

chunks = np.array_split(np.arange(len(i)), 16)
parts = Parallel(n_jobs=16, backend="threading")(
    delayed(paired_cosine_distances)(emb[i[c]], emb[j[c]]) for c in chunks
)
dist = np.concatenate(parts)
```

Either way, the result goes back onto the graph afterwards:

```python
g_dist = graph.Graph(pd.Series(dist, index=adj.index, name="weight"))
```

Two caveats on the chunked version:

- **Chunk boundaries:** `array_split` cuts the list of neighbour pairs into 16 equal blocks, so a polygon's pairs can be split between two neighbouring chunks. That doesn't affect the result. If you'd rather have exact "16 groups of polygons", I'd split on the focal codes instead, which is one more line.

- **Readability:** the chunked version is still short, but the `Parallel`/`delayed` part is the bit a reader of a #30DayMapChallenge notebook would have to stop and work out, for a saving of under a second.

@@markdown
## Neighbour dissimilarity

We measure how different each area is from each of its neighbours using **cosine distance** between their 2024 embedding vectors (1 − cosine similarity, from 0 for identical directions to 2 for opposite). Cosine ignores vector length, which in these area averages partly reflects how mixed the land cover is, and is the comparison AlphaEarth embeddings are designed for. Neighbours come from the fuzzy-contiguity graph `g`, i.e. queen contiguity plus the overlapping England–Scotland border pairs.

The 46,832 areas are split into 16 groups (one per core), and each group&#x27;s distances to all its neighbours are computed on a separate thread. NumPy releases Python&#x27;s global interpreter lock while it computes, so threads share the arrays without copying them. The results are reassembled into the order of `g.adjacency` and stored as the weights of a new graph, `g_dist`.
@@code
%%time
from joblib import Parallel, delayed
from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import paired_cosine_distances

N_CHUNKS = 16

adj = g.adjacency
focal = adj.index.get_level_values(&quot;focal&quot;)
i = lsoas.index.get_indexer(focal)  # row of each focal area in emb
j = lsoas.index.get_indexer(adj.index.get_level_values(&quot;neighbor&quot;))

# Rows of adj belonging to each group of focal areas
rows = [np.flatnonzero(focal.isin(codes)) for codes in np.array_split(lsoas.index, N_CHUNKS)]

parts = Parallel(n_jobs=N_CHUNKS, backend=&quot;threading&quot;)(
    delayed(paired_cosine_distances)(emb[i[r]], emb[j[r]]) for r in rows
)
dist = np.empty(len(adj))
for r, d in zip(rows, parts):
    dist[r] = d

g_dist = graph.Graph(pd.Series(dist, index=adj.index, name=&quot;weight&quot;))
@@code
# Sanity checks: every link covered once, identical to the serial calculation, same structure as g
assert sum(len(r) for r in rows) == len(adj)
assert np.allclose(dist, paired_cosine_distances(emb[i], emb[j]))
assert g_dist.n_edges == g.n_edges and (g_dist.unique_ids == g.unique_ids).all()

g_dist.adjacency.describe()
@@code
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
ax.hist(g_dist.adjacency, bins=200, color=&quot;0.3&quot;)

from joblib import Parallel, delayed
from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import paired_cosine_distances

N_CHUNKS = 16

adj = g.adjacency
i = lsoas.index.get_indexer(adj.index.get_level_values(&quot;focal&quot;))  # row of each focal area in emb
j = lsoas.index.get_indexer(adj.index.get_level_values(&quot;neighbor&quot;))

# Assign each area to one of N_CHUNKS groups, then find the links whose focal area is in each group
area_chunk = np.repeat(np.arange(N_CHUNKS), [len(c) for c in np.array_split(np.arange(len(lsoas)), N_CHUNKS)])
link_chunk = area_chunk[i]
rows = [np.flatnonzero(link_chunk == k) for k in range(N_CHUNKS)]

parts = Parallel(n_jobs=N_CHUNKS, backend=&quot;threading&quot;)(
    delayed(paired_cosine_distances)(emb[i[r]], emb[j[r]]) for r in rows
)
dist = np.empty(len(adj))
for r, d in zip(rows, parts):
    dist[r] = d

g_dist = graph.Graph(pd.Series(dist, index=adj.index, name=&quot;weight&quot;))
EOF

**How it works:** the 46,832 areas are split into 16 groups by focal area, one per core. **Checks:** a separate cell confirms that every pair was computed exactly once, that the result matches a single-threaded calculation, and that `g_dist` has the same areas and links as `g`.

<div class="note prompt" id="p-18"><div class="note-meta"><a href="#p-18">#18</a> · Wed 4 Nov, 13:23</div><div class="note-text">ok now let&#x27;s think about how a distance between the focal area and its neighbors would work. Two thoughts: 1) we get the distances between i and every j in the neighborhood, and then average it; 2) we average the embedding of the neighbors and then the distance. Thoughts?</div></div>
```


::: {.reply}
Both are reasonable, but they measure different things. I'd compute both, since each takes a line or two and they're more useful side by side.

**1. Average of the distances, mean(d(i, j)):** "how different is this area from each of its neighbours, on average?"

- It counts an area as dissimilar when it differs from its neighbours one by one. That includes areas that sit between neighbours that differ from each other.

- Example: a farmland area with town on one side and moorland on the other scores high, even if farmland is a fair halfway point between the two.

- It uses `g_dist` directly: the mean of each area's distances to its neighbours.

**2. Distance to the averaged neighbour, d(i, mean(j)):** "how different is this area from its surroundings taken as a whole?"

- This is the embedding version of a spatial lag: the row-standardised graph's lag applied to `emb` gives one averaged vector per area, which is then compared with the area's own vector.

- Differences among the neighbours tend to cancel out in the average, so the farmland example above scores lower. What scores high is a genuine outlier: an area unlike anything around it, like `E01030745` from the last table.

- One subtlety: averaging very different neighbours gives a blurred, mixed vector. A mixed area of its own can then look close to its surroundings even though it matches none of them individually.

**How they relate:** with these embeddings, option 2 should come out at or below option 1 for nearly every area. The gap between them roughly measures how much the neighbours differ from each other. That gives three useful cases:

| Option 1 | Option 2 | Reading |

|---|---|---|

| high | high | outlier, unlike all of its surroundings |

| high | low | sits between neighbours that differ from each other (an edge or transition) |

| low | low | uniform neighbourhood |

**Weighting:** both options give every neighbour equal weight. One alternative is weighting by the length of shared boundary, using `build_contiguity(..., by_perimeter=True)` on our graph. Another, for option 2 only, is weighting by neighbour area, so that the averaged neighbour reflects the actual land around the area. I'd start unweighted and revisit if small slivers of neighbouring areas turn out to distort results.

**Recommendation:** if we need one number for "most dissimilar area" maps, I'd use **option 2**, since it matches "unlike its surroundings" and is less sensitive to one odd neighbour. I'd also compute option 1, compare the two in a scatter plot, and look at the cases where they disagree.

Want me to add both to the notebook as a new subsection with a scatter plot comparing them?
:::

::: {.reply}
Both measures are short with the Graph API. I tested the pieces on a toy example, and `Graph.lag` accepts the full 2-D embeddings array directly.

**Option 1: average of the pairwise distances**

The distances are already stored as the weights of `g_dist`, so this is just a mean per area:

```python
mean_dist = g_dist.aggregate("mean")  # one value per focal area
```

`aggregate` groups the weights by focal area. It's the same as `g_dist.adjacency.groupby(level="focal").mean()`.

**Option 2: distance to the averaged neighbour**

```python
g_r = g.transform("r")    # row-standardise: each area's neighbour weights sum to 1
emb_lag = g_r.lag(emb)    # (46,832 × 64): average embedding of each area's neighbours
lag_dist = paired_cosine_distances(emb, emb_lag)
```

- `lag(emb)` returns a 46,832 × 64 array whose row *i* is the mean of the vectors of *i*'s neighbours. Underneath, this is one sparse matrix product, `g_r.sparse @ emb`.

- Row *i* of `emb_lag` lines up with row *i* of `emb`, because we checked earlier that `g.unique_ids` matches `lsoas.index`.

- We use `g`, not `g_dist`, since the averaging needs equal weights, not distances.

**Notes:**

- **No parallelism needed here:** option 2 compares only 46,832 pairs, a sixth of the earlier 272k, so it takes milliseconds serially. Reusing the 16-group threaded scheme would add complexity for nothing. I'll keep it serial unless you'd rather have the two calculations look alike.

- **Output:** both results go into one table `neighbourhood`, indexed by area code, with columns `mean_dist` (option 1) and `lag_dist` (option 2). It includes a check that `lag_dist <= mean_dist` for nearly every area, as argued earlier, and reports any exceptions.

- **Comparison:** summary statistics for both, a scatter plot of `mean_dist` against `lag_dist`, and their rank correlation.

All of this would go into a new subsection, **Dissimilarity from the whole neighbourhood**, under **Neighbour dissimilarity**. Shall I add it?

<details class="steps"><summary><b>2 steps</b> · Add neighbourhood dissimilarity subsection and execute · Read scratchpad/nbout/b8249f7d6ff02b10.png</summary><details class="tool"><summary><span class="tool-name">Bash</span> Add neighbourhood dissimilarity subsection and execute</summary><pre class="tool-in">nb cell add gdsl30dmc.ipynb --source - &lt;&lt;&#x27;EOF&#x27;
@@markdown
### Dissimilarity from the whole neighbourhood

Two ways to score how different an area is from its neighbourhood as a whole, using equal weights for every neighbour:

- **`mean_dist`**: the average of the cosine distances to each neighbour, i.e. how different the area is from its neighbours one by one. Taken from the weights of `g_dist`.
- **`lag_dist`**: the cosine distance to the *average neighbour*, i.e. how different the area is from its surroundings taken together. The average neighbour is the spatial lag of the embeddings on the row-standardised graph.

Since averaging neighbours tends to cancel out their differences, `lag_dist` should be at most `mean_dist` for nearly every area. The gap between the two is roughly how much the neighbours differ among themselves.
@@code
emb_lag = g.transform(&quot;r&quot;).lag(emb)  # row i = mean embedding of area i&#x27;s neighbours

neighbourhood = pd.DataFrame({
    &quot;mean_dist&quot;: g_dist.aggregate(&quot;mean&quot;).reindex(lsoas.index),
    &quot;lag_dist&quot;: paired_cosine_distances(emb, emb_lag),
}, index=lsoas.index)

assert neighbourhood.notna().all().all()
print(&quot;Areas where lag_dist &gt; mean_dist:&quot;, (neighbourhood.lag_dist &gt; neighbourhood.mean_dist).sum())
print(&quot;Spearman rank correlation:&quot;, round(neighbourhood.corr(method=&quot;spearman&quot;).iloc[0, 1], 3))
neighbourhood.describe()
@@code
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 6))
hb = ax.hexbin(neighbourhood.mean_dist, neighbourhood.lag_dist, gridsize=120, bins=&quot;log&quot;, cmap=&quot;viridis&quot;, mincnt=1)
lim = neighbourhood.max().max() * 1.02
ax.plot([0, lim], [0, lim], color=&quot;0.5&quot;, lw=0.8, ls=&quot;--&quot;)
ax.set_xlim(0, lim); ax.set_ylim(0, lim); ax.set_aspect(&quot;equal&quot;)
ax.set_xlabel(&quot;mean_dist: average distance to each neighbour&quot;)
ax.set_ylabel(&quot;lag_dist: distance to the average neighbour&quot;)
fig.colorbar(hb, ax=ax, shrink=0.8, label=&quot;Areas (log scale)&quot;);
EOF

import numpy as np, pandas as pd, geopandas as gpd

emb = np.ascontiguousarray(l[band].to_numpy())
adj = g.adjacency

print(nb.sort_values(&quot;mean_dist&quot;, ascending=False).head(5)); print(nb.sort_values(&quot;lag_dist&quot;, ascending=False).head(5))
nb.to_parquet(f&quot;{S}/neighbourhood.parquet&quot;); pairs.to_frame().to_parquet(f&quot;{S}/pairs.parquet&quot;)
l[[&quot;geometry&quot;]].to_parquet(f&quot;{S}/geoms.parquet&quot;)
EOF

Inside them the satellite imagery is at full brightness, so the area of interest stands out: Heathrow and the housing to the south-east are dimmed, while the reservoirs and the neighbouring estates stay bright.

How it works: I take the map frame as a rectangle and subtract the merged outline of the focal area and its neighbours. What's left is the "everything else" shape, drawn in black at 50% opacity. It sits above the imagery but below the red and yellow outlines, so the lines stay crisp. It's a few lines in `template.py` and needs nothing new.

What you could tweak:

- **Darkness:** 50% opacity is a middle setting. About 35% keeps more context visible; 60–65% makes the area of interest pop more.

- **Colour:** I could fade to white instead of black. That gives a washed-out look, though the yellow outlines would then need a darker edge.

- **Inset:** it still overlaps a corner of one neighbour here. With the darkened surroundings, the top-right corner would often be emptier, so I could pick the corner automatically for each map.

## Mapping the most dissimilar areas

Each map shows a focal area and its neighbours over Esri satellite imagery (no API key needed). The imagery outside those areas is washed out towards white, the focal area is outlined in orange and its neighbours in teal. A small UK silhouette in the corner shows where it is. The colours are from [Imago](https://imago.ac.uk)&#x27;s palette (orange `#ff8f42`, teal `#03cea3`, indigo `#24226f`).

The UK silhouette comes from merging all areas. A direct merge of all 46k polygons takes minutes, so we merge each nation separately with GEOS&#x27;s fast `coverage_union`, which works when polygons tile without gaps or overlaps. Northern Ireland&#x27;s polygons don&#x27;t meet that requirement, so they fall back to a slower standard merge. We then join the four nations, drop holes and specks, and simplify.
@@code
%%time
import contextily as cx
import shapely
from matplotlib import patheffects as pe

def merge(geoms):
    try:
        return shapely.coverage_union_all(geoms)
    except shapely.errors.GEOSException:  # polygons not cleanly tiled
        return shapely.union_all(shapely.simplify(geoms, 200))

uk_merged = shapely.union_all([merge(sub.values) for _, sub in lsoas.geometry.groupby(nation)])
uk_outline = gpd.GeoSeries([shapely.MultiPolygon([
    shapely.Polygon(p.exterior).simplify(1500) for p in shapely.get_parts(uk_merged) if p.area &gt; 20e6
])], crs=lsoas.crs)
@@code
IMAGO = {&quot;orange&quot;: &quot;#ff8f42&quot;, &quot;teal&quot;: &quot;#03cea3&quot;, &quot;indigo&quot;: &quot;#24226f&quot;}
WASH = 0.55  # share of white blended into imagery outside the focal area and its neighbours


def plot_focal(code, ax=None):
    &quot;&quot;&quot;Satellite map of area `code` and its neighbours, with the surroundings washed out and a UK locator.&quot;&quot;&quot;
    focal = lsoas.loc[[code], [&quot;geometry&quot;]]
    nbrs = lsoas.loc[g.neighbors[code], [&quot;geometry&quot;]]
    x0, y0, x1, y1 = pd.concat([focal, nbrs]).total_bounds
    pad = 0.05 * max(x1 - x0, y1 - y0)
    x0, y0, x1, y1 = x0 - pad, y0 - pad, x1 + pad, y1 + pad

    # Imagery, reprojected to British National Grid, washed out outside the areas
    bounds = gpd.GeoSeries([shapely.box(x0, y0, x1, y1)], crs=lsoas.crs).to_crs(3857).total_bounds
    img, ext = cx.bounds2img(*bounds, source=cx.providers.Esri.WorldImagery)
    img, ext = cx.warp_tiles(img, ext, t_crs=lsoas.crs)

## 2026-11-04 — Neighbourhood dissimilarity: mean_dist vs lag_dist

Two per-area scores, with equal weights for every neighbour: `mean_dist` = mean of the cosine distances to each neighbour
(`g_dist.aggregate(&quot;mean&quot;)`); `lag_dist` = cosine distance to the average neighbour embedding
(`g.transform(&quot;r&quot;).lag(emb)`). `lag_dist &lt;= mean_dist` for every area. Spearman rank correlation 0.84. Medians 0.046 vs 0.017, max 0.456 vs
0.438. In the scatter plot, areas near the diagonal are outliers (unlike all their surroundings); areas well below it are
transitions (their neighbours differ from each other). Also built `most_dissimilar`: each area&#x27;s single most dissimilar
neighbour and the distance to it.

**Top area on both measures: `E01030745`**, a pair of reservoir basins just south of Heathrow, surrounded by
housing/industry/airport (distances to those neighbours 0.39–0.54); its only similar neighbour (0.16) is the large reservoir
to the west. Expect other water/coast cases near the top of the ranking.

## 2026-11-04 — Map template (style &quot;C1&quot;)

Iterated in the scratchpad: map of a focal area + its neighbours over satellite imagery, comparing
4 fades (dark, washed, greyscale, navy) × 5 line palettes, then an Imago-palette grid (colours taken from
imago.ac.uk CSS: indigo `#24226f`/`#181651`, orange `#ff8f42`, teal `#03cea3`, lilac `#a9afff`, grey-lavender
`#8c91a8`, amber `#ffaf39`). **Chosen: C1** = Esri.WorldImagery; outside the focal area + neighbours washed to
white (55%); focal outline orange, neighbours teal, both with a faint dark outline; UK locator inset with no box
in Imago indigo with an orange dot.

**Implementation** (notebook, `plot_focal(code)`): fetch tiles once with `cx.bounds2img` and reproject to EPSG:27700
with `cx.warp_tiles`. The wash is applied to the image pixels with a mask from `shapely.contains_xy` against the merged
outline of the focal area and its neighbours (this also allows effects like greyscale, which an overlay polygon can&#x27;t do).
Attribution uses the provider&#x27;s own string.

**UK outline for the inset:** merging all 46k polygons took ~8 min. `shapely.coverage_union_all` on everything fails
(the polygons overlap at national borders), so: merge each nation with coverage union (England 0.4 s, Scotland 3 s, Wales
&lt;0.1 s; Northern Ireland isn&#x27;t cleanly tiled → falls back to `union_all` on 200 m-simplified polygons), then join the four
nations, drop holes and parts under 20 km², and simplify by 1.5 km. ~26 s total.

from matplotlib import font_manager

# Official Imago palette (brand guidelines); &quot;imago_grey&quot; is the Imago data service colour
IMAGO = {&quot;navy&quot;: &quot;#24226F&quot;, &quot;grey&quot;: &quot;#B8BCD1&quot;, &quot;green&quot;: &quot;#03CEA3&quot;, &quot;orange&quot;: &quot;#FF8F42&quot;,
         &quot;light_grey&quot;: &quot;#E2E5F3&quot;, &quot;blue&quot;: &quot;#1877CF&quot;, &quot;dark_grey&quot;: &quot;#8C91A8&quot;, &quot;white&quot;: &quot;#FFFFFF&quot;,
         &quot;imago_grey&quot;: &quot;#4A4A49&quot;}
WASH = 0.55  # share of white blended into imagery outside the focal area and its neighbours

# Imago&#x27;s brand font, Figtree (static TTFs from github.com/erikdkennedy/figtree, OFL licence)
for weight in [&quot;Regular&quot;, &quot;Bold&quot;]:
    font_manager.fontManager.addfont(f&quot;fonts/Figtree-{weight}.ttf&quot;)

# Polaroid card: square photo with even white borders and a deeper caption strip (sizes in inches)
CARD_W, BORDER, STRIP = 8, 0.45, 1.6
CARD_H = CARD_W + STRIP


def plot_focal(code):
    &quot;&quot;&quot;Polaroid-style satellite card of area `code` and its neighbours, surroundings washed out, with a UK locator.&quot;&quot;&quot;
    focal = lsoas.loc[[code], [&quot;geometry&quot;]]
    nbrs = lsoas.loc[g.neighbors[code], [&quot;geometry&quot;]]
    x0, y0, x1, y1 = pd.concat([focal, nbrs]).total_bounds
    cx_, cy_, half = (x0 + x1) / 2, (y0 + y1) / 2, 0.55 * max(x1 - x0, y1 - y0)
    x0, y0, x1, y1 = cx_ - half, cy_ - half, cx_ + half, cy_ + half  # square frame

    # Imagery, reprojected to British National Grid, washed out outside the areas
    bounds = gpd.GeoSeries([shapely.box(x0, y0, x1, y1)], crs=lsoas.crs).to_crs(3857).total_bounds
    img, ext = cx.bounds2img(*bounds, source=cx.providers.Esri.WorldImagery)
    img, ext = cx.warp_tiles(img, ext, t_crs=lsoas.crs)
    rgb = img[..., :3] / 255
    h, w = rgb.shape[:2]
    xx, yy = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(ext[0], ext[1], w), np.linspace(ext[3], ext[2], h))
    inside = shapely.contains_xy(pd.concat([focal, nbrs]).union_all(), xx, yy)[..., None]
    rgb = np.where(inside, rgb, rgb * (1 - WASH) + WASH)

    fig = plt.figure(figsize=(CARD_W, CARD_H), facecolor=IMAGO[&quot;white&quot;])
    fig.patch.set_edgecolor(IMAGO[&quot;light_grey&quot;]); fig.patch.set_linewidth(2)
    side = (CARD_W - 2 * BORDER) / CARD_W

**What the cards show:** ranks 2–5 are the reverse of the reservoir case. Each is a small built-up area (a town centre or village core) inside a few large, mostly green rural neighbours:

- **N20003012:** a small built-up block in farmland in Northern Ireland.

- **W01001286:** a valley town in Wales surrounded by moorland and forestry.

- **N20002748:** a small coastal settlement on a farmed peninsula in Northern Ireland.

- **E01026177:** a dense housing area next to woodland and open land in eastern England.

I've only judged these from the imagery; I haven't checked the place names.

**Two things I noticed:**

1. **The ranking may favour areas with few neighbours.** Ranks 2–5 have only 2–4 neighbours each, against a typical 6. With so few, the average depends on just a handful of pairs, so one sharp contrast can push an area to the top. That's worth checking before we read too much into the ranking: we could look at how scores vary with the number of neighbours, or require a minimum number of neighbours.

2. **The focal area can be tiny on the card.** The frame fits the focal area and all its neighbours, so when the neighbours are large rural areas, the focal area ends up very small, as in N20003012 and N20002748. An option is to frame tighter around the focal area and let large neighbours run off the edge of the photo.

nb cell add gdsl30dmc.ipynb --source - &lt;&lt;&#x27;EOF&#x27;
@@markdown
## Most dissimilar neighbouring pairs

Instead of scoring an area against its whole neighbourhood, we now look at individual pairs of neighbours: two areas that share a border and look most unlike each other from space. Each pair appears twice in `g_dist` (A→B and B→A, with the same distance), so we keep one row per pair and rank them by cosine distance.
@@code
pairs = g_dist.adjacency.reset_index().rename(columns={&quot;focal&quot;: &quot;area_a&quot;, &quot;neighbor&quot;: &quot;area_b&quot;, &quot;weight&quot;: &quot;distance&quot;})
pairs = pairs[pairs.area_a &lt; pairs.area_b].sort_values(&quot;distance&quot;, ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True)

print(f&quot;{len(pairs):,} unique pairs&quot;)
pairs[&quot;distance&quot;].describe()
@@code
top_pairs = pairs.head(20)
print(&quot;Distinct areas among the top 20 pairs:&quot;, pd.unique(top_pairs[[&quot;area_a&quot;, &quot;area_b&quot;]].values.ravel()).size)
print(&quot;Most frequent areas in the top 20:&quot;)
print(pd.Series(top_pairs[[&quot;area_a&quot;, &quot;area_b&quot;]].values.ravel()).value_counts().head(5).to_string())
top_pairs
EOF

::: {.reply}
Both ideas are worth trying, and they combine well: the clusters give us a vocabulary of land types, and the city filter narrows where we look. I'd start with idea 2, because it needs no extra data and directly tackles the "built-up versus open land every time" problem.

**Idea 1: restrict to cities**

- **Pros:** cheap once we have boundaries, and it should surface urban contrasts: a park against dense terraces, docks against housing, a rail yard against a housing estate.

- **Needs city boundaries, which we don't have.** Options:

  - **Recommended:** the ONS lookup from areas to local authorities, which lets us filter on, say, the 33 London boroughs or Liverpool. Scotland and Northern Ireland have their own equivalent lookups.
  - **More precise:** ONS built-up area polygons, which match where a city physically ends rather than its administrative edge.
  - **Quickest:** a radius around each city centre. No download, but crude.
- **Caveat:** cities contain parks, reservoirs and rivers, so built-up-versus-open contrasts won't disappear. They'll just be urban ones. The reservoir isn't technically in London: it's in Spelthorne, just outside it.

**Idea 2: cluster, then search at the cluster level**

- **a. Clustering:** k-means with k=100 on the 64-band embeddings takes seconds at this size. I'd first scale each vector to length 1. That makes k-means effectively cluster by cosine similarity, matching the distance we've used so far.

- **b. Interpreting clusters:** there's no land-cover label to check against, so interpretation has to be visual. For each cluster, I'd make a contact sheet of satellite thumbnails of its 9 most typical areas, which suits the Polaroid theme.

  - **Labelling 100 by eye is a lot of work.** I'd also merge the 100 clusters into about 10–15 families, using Ward clustering on their centres, so we can label families first and drill in where it matters.
  - **My labels would be guesses** read from the imagery, so you'd want to sanity-check them.
- **c. Searching by cluster:** this is where it gets interesting. Two ways:

  - **One example per contrast type:** label every neighbouring pair by its two clusters, then keep only the most extreme pair for each cluster combination. The final ranking then spans different kinds of contrast instead of 20 variations on housing next to water. "The industrial estate next to the most different landscape" is a filter on this: pairs where one side is an industrial-looking cluster, ranked by distance.
  - **Surprising neighbours:** count how often each pair of clusters actually sits side by side, compared with chance. Clusters that are adjacent less often than expected, or never, point to unusual juxtapositions, which is a different notion of "interesting" from raw distance.
- **Caveat:** two-thirds of the areas are English LSOAs, mostly urban, so many of the 100 clusters will be shades of residential. That's fine, as it's exactly what we need to tell urban types apart.

**Proposed order:**

1. A new section, **Clustering the embeddings**: k-means at k=100 (with a quick check of a few other values of k), the cluster families, and contact sheets for each family.

2. You review the contact sheets and we agree labels.

3. A cluster-level search, showing one example per contrast type plus the surprising-neighbours view, then cards.

4. Idea 1 as a filter on top, once we pick a boundary source and a list of cities.

Two questions before I start: is k=100 fixed, or should I compare a few values first? And for idea 1 later, which cities do you want, and should I use the local-authority lookup?
:::

::: {.reply}
The data doesn't point to a natural number, so the choice comes down to what we'll do with the clusters. I'd start with **k=20**.

**Scan results** (all 46,844 areas, vectors scaled to length 1, about 5 s per k):

| k | silhouette | smallest cluster | largest cluster |

|---|---|---|---|

| 5 | 0.29 | 5,491 | 13,410 |

| 10 | 0.25 | 2,768 | 9,406 |

| 20 | 0.21 | 835 | 3,584 |

| 30 | 0.19 | 562 | 2,582 |

| 50 | 0.18 | **89** | 1,724 |

| 100 | 0.15 | 67 | 883 |

Silhouette measures how well separated the clusters are, from −1 to 1, with higher better.

**What this says:**

- **No natural number of clusters:** silhouette falls steadily as k grows, with no peak and no elbow. The embeddings form continuous gradients (rural → suburban → dense urban), so any k is a way of slicing a continuum. Statistics won't settle it; interpretability should.

- **Rare land types appear somewhere between k=40 and k=50:** the smallest cluster drops from 315 areas to 89. A tiny cluster at higher k is likely a rare type such as water, airports, quarries or large industrial sites. Those rare types are exactly what makes a contrast interesting, so we shouldn't lose them entirely.

**Why k=20:**

- **Labelling is feasible:** 20 clusters can be checked by eye in an afternoon. At 100 we'd be guessing.

- **The contrast types stay manageable:** 20 clusters give 190 possible pairs of cluster types, few enough to browse. 100 give 4,950.

- **Every cluster is substantial,** with at least 835 areas, so each label describes something common.

**To keep the rare types,** I'd also fit k=50 and record each area's k=50 cluster alongside its k=20 one. We label the 20 broad groups, and the small k=50 clusters show up as named rarities ("water", "airport") that we can label separately. That gives broad groups for the overall structure and fine clusters for the unusual places. It's simpler than the merge-100-clusters-into-families idea I suggested before.

If you agree, I'll start the **Clustering the embeddings** section with k=20 (plus the k=50 detail), including this scan and contact sheets of typical areas per cluster for us to label.

The silhouette is built by merging each nation&#x27;s areas, using GEOS&#x27;s fast `coverage_union` where the polygons tile cleanly, then simplifying. # #30DayMapChallenge — Day 10: clustering the embeddings

The first notebook (`gdsl30dmc.ipynb`) found the UK&#x27;s most dissimilar neighbouring small areas, but the top results were nearly always built-up land against open land. Here we cluster the 2024 AlphaEarth embeddings into groups of similar areas, interpret the groups visually, and then search for contrasts between *types* of place, e.g. the industrial estate next to the most different landscape. Shared data loading, contiguity and Polaroid cards come from `gdsl30dmc_tools.py`.
EOF
nb cell add gdsl30dmc_clusters.ipynb --source - &lt;&lt;&#x27;EOF&#x27;
@@markdown
## Setup

Libraries for this notebook: `scikit-learn` for k-means and silhouette scores, plus the shared `gdsl30dmc_tools` module. `autoreload` picks up edits to the module without restarting the kernel.
@@code
%load_ext autoreload
%autoreload 2

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score

import gdsl30dmc_tools as tools
@@markdown
## Reading data

We load the 2024 areas and build the same neighbour graph as in the first notebook: fuzzy contiguity, which is queen contiguity plus the overlapping England–Scotland border pairs. We drop the 12 island areas with no neighbours. Each embedding vector is scaled to length 1, so that k-means, which works with Euclidean distance, effectively groups areas by cosine similarity, the same measure used in the first notebook.
@@code
%%time
YEAR = 2024
lsoas = tools.load_areas(YEAR)
g = tools.contiguity(lsoas)
lsoas, g = tools.drop_isolates(lsoas, g)

emb = np.ascontiguousarray(lsoas[tools.band_columns(lsoas)].to_numpy())
emb_unit = emb / np.linalg.norm(emb, axis=1, keepdims=True)
uk_outline = tools.uk_outline(lsoas)

print(f&quot;{len(lsoas):,} areas | {g.n_edges:,} links | embeddings {emb_unit.shape}&quot;)
EOF

@@markdown
## Choosing the number of clusters

Before fixing k, we fit k-means for a range of values and record two things: the silhouette score (how well separated the clusters are, from −1 to 1, computed with cosine distance on a 10,000-area sample) and the size of the smallest cluster. There&#x27;s no single right k here: the aim is a number of groups we can label by eye that still keeps rare land types visible.
@@code
%%time
KS = [5, 8, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 40, 50, 75, 100]
sample = np.random.default_rng(0).choice(len(emb_unit), 10_000, replace=False)

rows = []
for k in KS:
    labels = KMeans(k, n_init=3, random_state=0).fit_predict(emb_unit)
    sizes = np.bincount(labels)
    rows.append({&quot;k&quot;: k, &quot;silhouette&quot;: silhouette_score(emb_unit[sample], labels[sample], metric=&quot;cosine&quot;),
                 &quot;smallest&quot;: sizes.min(), &quot;largest&quot;: sizes.max()})
k_scan = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index(&quot;k&quot;)
k_scan.round(3)
@@code
fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.5))
k_scan[&quot;silhouette&quot;].plot(ax=ax1, marker=&quot;o&quot;, color=tools.IMAGO[&quot;navy&quot;])
ax1.set_ylabel(&quot;Silhouette (cosine)&quot;)
k_scan[&quot;smallest&quot;].plot(ax=ax2, marker=&quot;o&quot;, color=tools.IMAGO[&quot;orange&quot;], logy=True)
ax2.set_ylabel(&quot;Smallest cluster (areas, log scale)&quot;)
for ax in (ax1, ax2):
    ax.axvline(20, color=tools.IMAGO[&quot;dark_grey&quot;], ls=&quot;--&quot;, lw=0.8)
    ax.set_xlabel(&quot;k&quot;)
fig.tight_layout()
@@markdown
Silhouette falls steadily as k grows, with no peak or elbow: the embeddings form continuous gradients (rural → suburban → dense urban) rather than separate clumps, so any k slices a continuum. Very small clusters first appear between k=40 and k=50, which likely marks rare land types (water, airports, quarries) splitting off. We therefore use **k=20** to label the main groups (190 possible pairs of cluster types, every cluster with several hundred areas or more) and also record each area&#x27;s **k=50** cluster, to keep the rare types visible.
EOF

@@markdown
## Clustering the embeddings

We fit k-means at two levels: **k=20** for the main land types we&#x27;ll label by eye, and **k=100** for a finer split that should separate rarer types. We use 10 random starts per fit for stability, and number the clusters in each level by size (0 = largest), so the numbering stays meaningful. The labels are saved to `data/clusters_2024.parquet` for reuse.
@@code
%%time
def fit_kmeans(k, seed=0):
    km = KMeans(k, n_init=10, random_state=seed).fit(emb_unit)
    order = np.argsort(-np.bincount(km.labels_))  # old label of the largest cluster first
    relabel = np.empty(k, int)
    relabel[order] = np.arange(k)
    return relabel[km.labels_], km.cluster_centers_[order]

c20, centres20 = fit_kmeans(20)
c100, centres100 = fit_kmeans(100)
clusters = pd.DataFrame({&quot;c20&quot;: c20, &quot;c100&quot;: c100}, index=lsoas.index)
clusters.to_parquet(tools.DATA_DIR / f&quot;clusters_{YEAR}.parquet&quot;)

print(&quot;k=20 sizes:&quot;, np.bincount(c20).tolist())
print(&quot;k=100 sizes: min&quot;, np.bincount(c100).min(), &quot;| median&quot;, int(np.median(np.bincount(c100))), &quot;| max&quot;, np.bincount(c100).max())
@@markdown
### How the two levels nest

k-means fits the two levels independently, so a fine cluster need not sit inside a single coarse one. For each k=100 cluster, we record which k=20 cluster most of its areas belong to and how large that share is. High shares mean the fine level mostly subdivides the coarse one, which makes the two levels easier to read together.
@@code
nest = pd.crosstab(clusters.c100, clusters.c20)
fine = pd.DataFrame({
    &quot;size&quot;: nest.sum(axis=1),
    &quot;main_c20&quot;: nest.idxmax(axis=1),
    &quot;share&quot;: (nest.max(axis=1) / nest.sum(axis=1)).round(2),
})
print(&quot;Share of each k=100 cluster inside its main k=20 cluster:&quot;)
print(fine[&quot;share&quot;].describe().round(2).to_string())
print(&quot;\nk=100 clusters per k=20 cluster:&quot;)
print(fine.groupby(&quot;main_c20&quot;).size().to_string())

def _washed_imagery(frame, crs, keep, wash=WASH):
    &quot;&quot;&quot;Esri satellite imagery for `frame` (x0, y0, x1, y1 in `crs`), reprojected to `crs` and washed out towards
    white outside the geometry `keep`. Returns an RGB array and its extent.&quot;&quot;&quot;
    bounds = gpd.GeoSeries([shapely.box(*frame)], crs=crs).to_crs(3857).total_bounds
    img, ext = cx.bounds2img(*bounds, source=cx.providers.Esri.WorldImagery)
    img, ext = cx.warp_tiles(img, ext, t_crs=crs)
    rgb = img[..., :3] / 255
    h, w = rgb.shape[:2]
    xx, yy = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(ext[0], ext[1], w), np.linspace(ext[3], ext[2], h))
    inside = shapely.contains_xy(keep, xx, yy)[..., None]
    return np.where(inside, rgb, rgb * (1 - wash) + wash), ext

@@markdown
## What the clusters look like

To interpret each k=20 cluster, we look at its six most typical areas: those whose embedding is closest (highest cosine similarity) to the cluster centre. Each is shown as a satellite thumbnail with the area outlined and its surroundings washed out. The sheets are saved to `figures/clusters/` so we can review them side by side and agree labels.
@@code
def typical(level_labels, centres, cluster, n=6):
    &quot;&quot;&quot;Codes of the n areas in `cluster` closest to its centre (cosine similarity).&quot;&quot;&quot;
    members = np.flatnonzero(level_labels == cluster)
    centre = centres[cluster] / np.linalg.norm(centres[cluster])
    best = members[np.argsort(-(emb_unit[members] @ centre))[:n]]
    return lsoas.index[best].tolist()

typical20 = {c: typical(c20, centres20, c) for c in range(20)}
@@code
%%time
sheet_dir = tools.FIG_DIR / &quot;clusters&quot;
for c, codes in typical20.items():
    fig = tools.contact_sheet(lsoas, codes, f&quot;k=20 cluster {c} · {np.sum(c20 == c):,} areas&quot;)
    tools.export_card(fig, f&quot;c20_{c:02d}&quot;, dpi=110, fig_dir=sheet_dir)
    plt.close(fig)
sorted(p.name for p in sheet_dir.glob(&quot;c20_*.png&quot;))[:3]
EOF

::: {.reply}
I've fitted the clusters at both levels and made contact sheets for the 20 broad clusters. Everything is in `gdsl30dmc_clusters.ipynb`, and it runs end to end in about 4.5 minutes, nearly all of it fetching satellite tiles.

**What's in the notebook:**

- **Clustering the embeddings:** k-means at k=20 and k=100, each with 10 random starts, numbered by size so that 0 is the largest. The labels are saved to `data/clusters_2024.parquet`.

  - **k=20:** clusters range from 837 to 3,628 areas.
  - **k=100:** clusters range from 71 to 869 areas.
- **How the two levels nest:** only loosely. A typical k=100 cluster has 61% of its areas in one k=20 cluster, so the fine clusters don't cleanly subdivide the broad ones. If we want a strict hierarchy, we could build the k=20 level by merging the k=100 clusters instead of fitting it separately.

- **What the clusters look like:** a contact sheet for each k=20 cluster showing its 6 most typical areas, saved in `figures/clusters/`. I've sent you the 20 sheets combined into 5 images. The thumbnail and contact-sheet helpers are now in the shared module.

- **Clusters by nation:** each cluster's share of areas in each nation, plus its median area size.

**Draft labels, from my reading of the imagery, for you to correct:**

| c20 | Draft label | Median area |

|---|---|---|

| 0 | suburban housing with green space | 0.41 km² |

| 1 | Scottish/NI urban housing estates and flats (60% Scotland, 29% NI) | 0.15 |

| 2 | suburban housing next to industry or an airfield | 0.33 |

| 3 | edge-of-town housing with fields | 0.68 |

| 4 | dense post-war estates with curving streets | 0.32 |

| 5 | Scottish/NI suburban and new-build housing at the countryside edge (71% Scotland) | 0.29 |

| 6 | suburban housing mixed with schools and retail | 0.36 |

| 7 | inner suburbs next to industry | 0.26 |

| 8 | **arable farmland**, large rural areas | 12.95 |

| 9 | dense inner-city housing, London-like | 0.18 |

| 10 | mixed farmland with villages | 9.22 |

| 11 | **pastoral farmland**: grass fields and hedgerows, all four nations | 11.66 |

| 12 | Scottish/NI dense urban housing (65% Scotland) | 0.16 |

| 13 | settlement edge: housing plus fields | 1.13 |

| 14 | small towns and villages with surrounding fields | 0.96 |

| 15 | **Victorian terraces** | 0.16 |

| 16 | dense inner urban: terraces and flats | 0.18 |

| 17 | **woodland, parkland and golf courses** on the urban fringe | 2.28 |

| 18 | **city centres**: high-density commercial | 0.13 |

| 19 | **uplands and moorland** (Scottish Highlands, Lake District) | 47.11 |

**What stands out:**

1. **About 12 of the 20 clusters are shades of residential.** That was expected, since most areas are urban LSOAs, but it leaves only a few non-residential types (city centres, farmland, woodland, uplands).

2. **There's no industrial or water cluster at this level.** Industrial estates appear only as context next to housing, so for your example, "the industrial estate next to the most different landscape", we'll need the k=100 level. I'd make contact sheets for its smallest clusters next, since that's where industry, water, airports and quarries should show up.

3. **Clusters 1, 5 and 12 are mostly Scottish and Northern Irish urban areas,** even though England has 72% of all areas. That could be real: building styles and roofing materials differ. It could also be a regional effect in the embeddings, or simply that Scottish Data Zones are smaller. It matters for the search, because a cross-border pair could score as dissimilar partly through this effect. I'd treat it as a caveat for now.

Two things I need from you:

1. Corrections or renames for any of the labels; once agreed, I'll store them in the notebook.

2. Whether to go ahead with contact sheets for the smallest k=100 clusters, to find the industrial, water and other rare types.

This is the contact sheet for k=20 cluster 18, the one I drafted as **"city centres"**. It has 1,180 areas, and the sheet shows the 6 closest to the cluster centre. The file is `figures/clusters/c20_18.png`.

On closer inspection, "city centres" is a bit too strong a label:

- **What they share:** small areas (0.08–0.40 km²) that are almost fully built up, with large flat-roofed blocks, flats, offices and institutional buildings. There are hardly any gardens and little of the regular terraced pattern you see in clusters 15 and 16.

- **Not all are central business districts:**

  - The top-left area sits beside what looks like a football stadium.
  - Top-right and bottom-middle are on a waterfront or docks.
  - Several look like dense inner-city mixed use: council blocks, campuses and offices.
- The only non-English example is `W01001695`, from Wales.

A more accurate label might be **"dense inner-city mixed use (flats, offices, institutions)"**. If you want true commercial cores like the City of London or Manchester's centre, they're probably a subset that only separates at k=100.

I can make a larger sheet for this cluster, say 12 or 24 areas, or a sheet of its k=100 sub-clusters, to check whether a pure city-centre type falls out.
:::

::: {.reply}
Yes. k=100 **cluster 95** is a much better fit for "city centres". I found it by checking which k=100 clusters known central areas fall into: all the City of London and central Manchester areas I tried land in cluster 95 or cluster 88. I've sent contact sheets of the 9 most typical areas in each.

**Cluster 95: business cores (133 areas)**

- Its typical areas look like high-rise office districts: the Thames-side City and Southwark around London Bridge, and tower clusters that appear to be Canary Wharf. The towers, big flat roofs and almost no green space are typical of a central business district.

- It includes City of London areas (`E01000001`, `…02`, `…05`, `E01032739`) and central Manchester (`E01033677`, `E01033658`).

- It's very small: median 0.11 km². 114 areas are in England, 17 in Scotland and 2 in Northern Ireland, so it presumably also picks up central Glasgow and Edinburgh, though I haven't checked which areas those are.

- Only 65% of its areas sit in k=20 cluster 18. This is the loose nesting showing up again: some business cores went to other broad clusters.

**Cluster 88: central mixed use (232 areas)**

- It sits entirely inside k=20 cluster 18.

- It's dense central fabric but not office towers: mansion blocks, institutions, rail stations and mixed streets. It looks like the inner West End and the edges of city centres.

- It also contains some City of London areas (`E01000003`, `E01032740`) and central Manchester areas (`E01033654`, `E01033664`), so there isn't a hard line between the two clusters.

**Suggested labels**

- k=100 cluster 95: **"business core: high-rise offices"**. Use this as the true city-centre type.

- k=100 cluster 88: **"central mixed use"**.

- k=20 cluster 18: rename to **"dense inner-city mixed use"**.

For the search, cluster 95 is a strong candidate for interesting pairs, such as a business core directly next to a residential estate or a park.
:::

::: {.reply}
I've made Polaroids for the five most dissimilar neighbouring pairs that include a business-core area (k=100 cluster 95). Orange is the business core and green is its neighbour. As with the earlier pair cards, no area appears twice. I've sent them as a grid.

| # | Pair | Distance | What the neighbour shows |

|---|---|---|---|

| 1 | `E01035620` → `E01035617` | **0.408** | Big open fields and a campus at the edge of the city centre, in northern England by the locator. |

| 2 | `E01034486` → `E01004401` | 0.289 | A large reservoir and industrial sheds next to a block of offices and flats, in London by the locator. |

| 3 | `S01017417` → `S01017432` | 0.268 | Dense Victorian tenements with a school pitch next to tower blocks. |

| 4 | `S01017414` → `S01017176` | 0.257 | A wooded riverside park with sports pitches next to the city-centre edge. |

| 5 | `S01017427` → `S01017433` | 0.254 | The central street grid next to a small block to its west. This one is weak. |

**What I take from these:**

- **Pairs 1, 2 and 4 are strong.** They each set the business core directly against open land, water or parkland.

- **Pair 1 stands out.** At 0.408 it is well ahead of the rest, which fall away quickly after it.

- **Pairs 3 and 5 are weaker:** core against other dense urban fabric. That's because cluster 95 has only 133 areas, so after the first few the remaining neighbours are mostly other dense city blocks.

- **Pairs 3–5 all look like Glasgow** (the Clyde and the central grid), which I haven't confirmed. It may be the Scotland-specific effect I flagged earlier, Scottish Data Zones being smaller, or just a coincidence.

These are scratch outputs in `scratchpad/` and aren't in the notebook yet. I can add a section to the clusters notebook and export these to `figures/`. I could also put place names in the captions instead of codes.

<details class="steps"><summary><b>5 steps</b> · Edit gdsl30dmc_tools.py · Run a shell command · …</summary><details class="tool"><summary><span class="tool-name">Edit</span> Edit gdsl30dmc_tools.py</summary><pre class="tool-in">return outline


def pair_distances(areas=None, g=None, cache=DATA_DIR / &quot;pair_distances_2024.parquet&quot;):
    &quot;&quot;&quot;Cosine distance for every neighbouring pair (each pair once, a &lt; b), cached to disk.

    Without `areas` and `g`, loads the cache (or builds it from the 2024 data, dropping isolates).
    &quot;&quot;&quot;
    if cache is not None and Path(cache).exists():
        return pd.read_parquet(cache)[&quot;dist&quot;]
    if areas is None or g is None:
        areas = load_areas()
        areas, g = drop_isolates(areas, contiguity(areas))
    adj = g.adjacency.reset_index()
    adj = adj[adj[&quot;focal&quot;] &lt; adj[&quot;neighbor&quot;]]
    emb = areas[band_columns(areas)].to_numpy()
    emb = emb / np.linalg.norm(emb, axis=1, keepdims=True)
    pos = pd.Series(np.arange(len(areas)), index=areas.index)
    dist = 1 - (emb[pos[adj[&quot;focal&quot;]]] * emb[pos[adj[&quot;neighbor&quot;]]]).sum(axis=1)
    out = pd.Series(dist, index=pd.MultiIndex.from_arrays([adj[&quot;focal&quot;], adj[&quot;neighbor&quot;]], names=[&quot;a&quot;, &quot;b&quot;]),
                    name=&quot;dist&quot;)
    if cache is not None:
        out.to_frame().to_parquet(cache)
    return out

::: {.reply}
You're right that they look alike: from above, both sides of those pairs are dense blocks with dark roofs. The embedding does tell them apart, but I wouldn't use them as cards.

**What the model sees**

- **Orange side (cluster 95):** `S01017417` and `S01017427` sit well inside the business-core cluster. Their most similar areas in the whole UK are other Glasgow core zones, and `S01017414`'s include London and Manchester cores. To the model they're office districts.

- **Green side (cluster 61):** `S01017432` and `S01017433` belong to a tenement and terrace housing cluster. 82% of its areas fall in the k=20 "Victorian terraces" cluster. Their most similar areas are neighbouring Glasgow zones (`S01017430`/`31`) and several Northern Irish areas, which I'd guess are Belfast but haven't checked.

So the 0.25–0.27 distance probably reflects the difference between commercial and residential use: building heights, flat versus pitched roofs, courtyard greenery. AlphaEarth mixes radar and multispectral inputs that respond to these. That's my reading, not something I've tested.

**Why the distance is still shaky**

1. **The areas are tiny.** These zones cover 0.03–0.10 km², which is only a few hundred 10 m pixels. Roads and edges weigh heavily in their average, so their vectors are noisier than most.

2. **The green areas are borderline members of their own cluster.** `S01017432` is further from its cluster centre than 98% of the other members, and `S01017433` is the furthest of all. They sit on the edge of the cluster, closer to the business core than to typical tenements.

3. **These are simply the extremes of a small pool.** Pairs touching Scottish business-core areas have a median distance of 0.036. The highest is 0.268, which is pair 3. Cluster 95 has only 133 areas, so after the first two cards we're down to subtle contrasts.

I've sent a contact sheet of the four Glasgow tenement zones next to their two closest Northern Irish matches. You can see they're the same type: courtyard blocks with dark roofs.

**My suggestion:** keep pairs 1, 2 and 4, which show visible contrasts (fields and campus, reservoir and sheds, riverside park). Drop 3 and 5. Going forward, I'd add a cut-off for "card-worthy" pairs: a minimum distance (for example the top 0.5% of pairs, about 0.27), a minimum area so tiny zones don't produce noise, or both.
:::

@@notebook {&quot;format&quot;:&quot;ai-notebook&quot;,&quot;metadata&quot;:{&quot;kernelspec&quot;:{&quot;display_name&quot;:&quot;GDS-2026-10-19_amd64&quot;,&quot;name&quot;:&quot;gds&quot;}}}

### Dissimilarity from the whole neighbourhood

Two ways to score how different an area is from its neighbourhood as a whole, using equal weights for every neighbour:

- **`mean_dist`**: the average of the cosine distances to each neighbour, i.e. how different the area is from its neighbours one by one. Taken from the weights of `g_dist`.
- **`lag_dist`**: the cosine distance to the *average neighbour*, i.e. how different the area is from its surroundings taken together. The average neighbour is the spatial lag of the embeddings on the row-standardised graph.

Since averaging neighbours tends to cancel out their differences, `lag_dist` should be at most `mean_dist` for nearly every area. The gap between the two is roughly how much the neighbours differ among themselves.

@@cell {&quot;cell_type&quot;:&quot;code&quot;,&quot;execution_count&quot;:15,&quot;id&quot;:&quot;105ff4a9-d0b4-4306-b60b-5cd11eda30ce&quot;,&quot;index&quot;:23}
```python
emb_lag = g.transform(&quot;r&quot;).lag(emb)  # row i = mean embedding of area i&#x27;s neighbours

neighbourhood = pd.DataFrame({
    &quot;mean_dist&quot;: g_dist.aggregate(&quot;mean&quot;).reindex(lsoas.index),
    &quot;lag_dist&quot;: paired_cosine_distances(emb, emb_lag),
}, index=lsoas.index)

assert neighbourhood.notna().all().all()
print(&quot;Areas where lag_dist &gt; mean_dist:&quot;, (neighbourhood.lag_dist &gt; neighbourhood.mean_dist).sum())
print(&quot;Spearman rank correlation:&quot;, round(neighbourhood.corr(method=&quot;spearman&quot;).iloc[0, 1], 3))
neighbourhood.describe()

Here are the top five business-core areas (k=100 cluster 95) ranked by `lag_dist`, each with the whole-UK `lag_dist` histogram underneath.

| # | Area | lag_dist | Rank among all areas | What you see |

|---|---|---|---|---|

| 1 | `E01034486` | **0.180** | top 0.29% | An office and flats block surrounded by reservoirs, sheds and a field. Same area as pair card 2. |

| 2 | `S01017173` | 0.096 | top 2.7% | A tiny Glasgow block (0.016 km²) whose neighbours are a motorway interchange, rail lines and sheds. |

| 3 | `E01034178` | 0.086 | top 3.7% | Riverside towers on the Thames, with low-rise housing and greenery behind them. |

| 4 | `E01033684` | 0.084 | top 3.9% | An office block among parkland, rail yards and a stadium. |

| 5 | `E01033874` | 0.076 | top 5.1% | Towers around a station, ringed by leafy housing. |

**What stands out:**

- **Only #1 is a real outlier.** After it, the cards fall to the top 3–5%, which the histogram line makes obvious.

- **Averaging dilutes the contrast.** `lag_dist` compares an area with the average of its neighbours. Business cores are usually surrounded by mixed fabric, so a park on one side and dense blocks on the other cancel out. On average, `lag_dist` is half of `mean_dist` (0.026 vs 0.053).

- **Few neighbours and tiny areas push the score up.** Most of these areas have only 2–3 neighbours, and #2 and #3 cover around 0.02 km² each. That's the same small-area noise we saw with the Glasgow pairs.

- **Cards 3–5 are still good pictures** even though their scores are modest. They show the "towers dropped into a neighbourhood" idea well. Card 3, with its towers by the river, is the most striking.

**Code changes:**

- `area_card` and `polaroid` now accept `hist="lag_dist"` or `hist="mean_dist"`, as well as `True` for pairs.

- The axis label adapts, for example "top 0.29% of 46,832 areas on lag_dist".

- A new `tools.neighbourhood_distances()` caches both measures to `data/neighbourhood_distances_2024.parquet`. It agrees with notebook 1: same summary statistics, and the maximum is still the Staines reservoir area.

::: {.reply}
The band chart fits. I've sent the two cards in four versions: the pair card (business core next to fields, 0.408) and the reservoir card (`lag_dist`, orange is the area and green is the average of its 3 neighbours), each with the band chart only and with the chart plus the histogram. The pair card with bars only is also attached at full size.

**How it's built:**

- New `emb=(orange_vector, green_vector)` argument on `polaroid`, `pair_card` and `area_card`.

- One column per band (1–64, numbered as in the data) with the orange and green bars side by side, and a thin zero line.

- **Band chart only:** it takes the histogram's slot, and the caption strip grows by 0.35 in so the bars have room.

- **Band chart and histogram together:** the strip grows by 0.9 in, so the card goes from 9.55 to 10.1 in tall. It still reads as a Polaroid with a deep bottom margin, and nothing overlaps.

**I'd use it instead of the histogram, not alongside it.** The two together make the caption busy and stretch the card. The histogram answers "how unusual is this?" with one mark, while the bars are texture you have to study.

**The bars show that the areas differ, but not clearly how.** 64 pairs of small bars mostly read as a pattern. You can pick out bands where the colours have opposite signs (around 3–5, 37 and 53), but there is no single standout band. That's expected: a cosine distance of 0.4 is spread across many bands, and the bands don't have meanings we could label.

To make it clearer, I'd replace the paired bars with **one bar per band showing the difference** (orange minus green), coloured orange or green by which area is higher. That halves the number of marks and makes the large gaps pop. I can also sort the bands by the size of the gap, which turns the chart into a profile that tapers off. Unsorted, it reads more like a fingerprint. Want me to try the difference version?
:::

I've made both options and sent them:

- **Strip close-ups:** the caption strip of the fields-and-campus pair card (0.408) at export resolution, with overlay on top and difference below.

- **Full cards:** the pair card and the reservoir `lag_dist` card in each style.

In the code, `emb_style=` now takes `"paired"`, `"overlay"` or `"diff"` on `polaroid`, `pair_card` and `area_card`. The default is still `"paired"`.

**Overlay:** both bars sit in the same slot at 60% opacity.

- It does what you described. Where the two areas agree, the bars merge into one solid block (bands 3, 6, 18, 49, 50). Where they disagree, you see separate pale orange and green tips, or bars pointing in opposite directions (4, 15, 24, 37).

- It keeps the actual values, so you can see whether both areas are high or low on a band.

- **Weakness:** orange over green blends to a muddy dark teal, so the shared part reads as a third colour rather than "same".

**Difference:** one bar per band (orange value minus green value), orange if the orange area is higher and green if the green area is.

- It's the cleaner of the two. Similar bands nearly disappear (2, 5, 6, 13, 33), and the largest gaps stand out (1, 16, 17, 36, 37, 39).

- It answers "where do they differ?" directly.

- **Weakness:** you lose the actual values. A band where both areas are strongly positive looks the same as one where both are near zero.

**My pick is the difference style.** It matches the story of each card best, and it's the calmest visually.

If you want to keep the overlay idea, one refinement would fix the muddy colour: draw the part the two areas share in light Imago grey, and only the excess in orange or green.
