::: {.reply}
The grey-shared version is now `emb_style="shared"`. I've sent its caption strip at export resolution and the two full cards (fields-and-campus pair, reservoir `lag_dist`).

**How it's drawn, band by band:**

- **Both areas on the same side of zero:** the part they share is a light Imago grey bar. Only the extra amount for whichever area goes further is in orange or green on top.

- **Opposite sides of zero:** no grey; orange goes one way and green the other, both from zero.

**How it reads:**

- Agreement is now neutral grey instead of the muddy teal from the transparency version. Bands 2, 6, 18, 50 and 54 are mostly grey: both areas are high, or both low.

- Disagreement is all colour: bands 1, 4, 16, 24, 37 and 52.

- You still see the actual values, so you can tell "both strongly positive" from "both near zero". The difference style lost that.

- **The amount of grey tracks similarity, so the two cards contrast.** The reservoir area against its average neighbour (`lag_dist` 0.180) has visibly more grey than the fields pair (0.408).

- **One thing to know:** a bar's height now mixes two meanings, the shared value and the gap. So it takes a moment longer to read than the difference style.

**My view:** this is the best of the four for a Polaroid. It's calm, mostly grey with colour only where it matters, and it explains itself without a legend, since orange and green already key the two areas in the title.

If you agree, I'd make `"shared"` the default `emb_style`. Then I'd add the business-core exploration to the clusters notebook as a section: k=100 cluster 95, top pairs and top `lag_dist` areas, exported with the band chart in place of the histogram.
:::

# #30DayMapChallenge — Day 10: clustering the embeddings

The first notebook (`gdsl30dmc.ipynb`) found the UK&#x27;s most dissimilar neighbouring small areas, but the top results were nearly always built-up land against open land. Here we cluster the 2024 AlphaEarth embeddings into groups of similar areas, interpret the groups visually, and then search for contrasts between *types* of place, e.g. the industrial estate next to the most different landscape. Shared data loading, contiguity and Polaroid cards come from `gdsl30dmc_tools.py`.


@@cell {&quot;cell_type&quot;:&quot;markdown&quot;,&quot;id&quot;:&quot;358c156c-fba8-4d90-9917-ef1fb182526e&quot;,&quot;index&quot;:1}

Pair cards were one-note (built-up vs open land every time). Two ideas: (1) restrict the search to cities (needs boundaries:

visually, then search at cluster level (top pair per cluster combination, and &quot;surprising neighbours&quot;, i.e. cluster pairs adjacent
less often than chance). Plan: do (2) first, then (1) as a filter on top.

````{=html}
### Business cores next to their most different neighbours

We take the cosine distance of every neighbouring pair (computed once and cached by `tools.pair_distances`) and keep the pairs that include a business-core area, with the core area listed first. As in the first notebook, we pick the top pairs greedily, skipping any pair that shares an area with one already chosen. The neighbour&#x27;s k=20 and k=100 clusters show what kind of place the core sits against.
@@code
pair_dist = tools.pair_distances(lsoas, g)
assert len(pair_dist) == g.n_edges // 2

core_pairs = pair_dist.reset_index()
in_a, in_b = core_pairs.a.isin(core), core_pairs.b.isin(core)
core_pairs = core_pairs[in_a | in_b]
swap = ~in_a[core_pairs.index]  # put the core area first
core_pairs.loc[swap, [&quot;a&quot;, &quot;b&quot;]] = core_pairs.loc[swap, [&quot;b&quot;, &quot;a&quot;]].to_numpy()
core_pairs = core_pairs.sort_values(&quot;dist&quot;, ascending=False)

used, picks = set(), []
for row in core_pairs.itertuples():
    if row.a in used or row.b in used:
        continue
    picks.append(row)
    used |= {row.a, row.b}
    if len(picks) == 5:
        break
top_core_pairs = pd.DataFrame(picks).drop(columns=&quot;Index&quot;).assign(
    nbr_c20=lambda d: clusters.c20[d.b].to_numpy(), nbr_c100=lambda d: clusters.c100[d.b].to_numpy(),
    rank=lambda d: [f&quot;top {(pair_dist &gt;= x).mean():.2%}&quot; for x in d.dist])
print(f&quot;{len(core_pairs):,} neighbouring pairs include a business-core area&quot;)
top_core_pairs.round(3)
@@markdown
````

::: {.reply}
I went through all 100 clusters. About 15 look like clearly defined kinds of place; the other 85 or so are shades of housing, farmland or rural–urban fringe. I've sent sheets showing the 9 most typical areas of each candidate.

These labels are my reading of satellite thumbnails, so treat them as a shortlist to check rather than confirmed labels.

**Clearly delimited entities**

| c100 | Entity | Areas | Median km² | Notes |

|---|---|---|---|---|

| **99** | **Reservoirs and inland water** | 71 | 1.13 | The clearest: large dark water bodies, usually with housing round the edge. The Staines reservoirs pair from notebook 1 belongs here. |

| **81** | **Industrial and transport land in towns** | 320 | 0.50 | Big sheds, rail yards, docks, stadiums. The closest thing to "industrial estates". |

| **50** | **Industrial and retail parks at the suburban edge** | 464 | 0.83 | Warehouse sheds mixed with housing; one looks like an airfield. |

| **42** | **Golf courses and leafy low-density suburbs** | 481 | 1.37 | Fairways are visible in at least 5 of the 9. |

| **91** | **Woodland and heathland** | 184 | 4.46 | Forests, wooded commons, large estates. 99% in England. |

| **90** | **Harbour and marina waterfront** | 199 | 0.52 | Coastal towns with marinas, quays and beaches. 92% in England. |

| **87** | **Port and coastal industrial towns** | 244 | 0.34 | Docks and industry by the sea. Mostly Scotland, England and Northern Ireland. |

| **93** | **Coastal fringe** | 174 | 0.92 | Dunes, saltmarsh, links golf, estuary edges. All four nations. |

| **95** | **Business cores** | 133 | 0.11 | Done. |

| **88** | **Central mixed use** | 232 | 0.12 | Mansion blocks, institutions, stations. |

**Clear landscape types (large rural areas)**

| c100 | Entity | Notes |

|---|---|---|

| 97 | Highland mountains and lochs | 285 km² median, 97% Scotland |

| 98 | Scottish islands and sea lochs | 100% Scotland |

| 94 | Scottish uplands | |

| 85 | English and Welsh uplands and moorland | |

| 92 | Welsh valleys | Moorland and forestry slopes with towns on the valley floor; 87% Wales |

**Partial or mixed: probably not worth targeting**

- **71: parkland, golf and woodland fringe.** It overlaps 42 and 91. 35% is in Wales.

- **86: countryside edge by an estuary or coast.** It has some golf and some estuary.

- **37: Scottish housing estates with large parks or playing fields.** One thumbnail is a racecourse.

- **33 and 96:** mixed small-town edges with no single entity.

**Not found at k=100:** airports, quarries, hospital or university campuses, cemeteries, caravan parks and stand-alone docks. These are probably smaller than a typical area, so they get averaged away within it. Airports would be the most likely of these to separate at a finer k.

**Next steps I'd suggest:** reservoirs (99), industrial (81 and 50), golf (42), woodland (91) and waterfront (90 and 87) are the strongest candidates for the cluster-level Polaroid search. I'd run the same pairs and `lag_dist` cards for each, with a minimum area to drop the tiny-area noise. None of this is in the notebook or the log yet; say if you want it recorded.
:::

::: {.reply}
I've sent 27 Polaroids: the top 3 pairs for each of the 9 entities, one image per entity. The entity area is orange and its neighbour green. As before, no area is used twice within an entity. I also added a filter: both areas must cover at least 0.05 km², which drops the tiny-area noise.

**What each entity turned up**

| Entity | Pairs | What stands out |

|---|---|---|

| **99 Reservoirs** | ranks 1, 15, 32 of all 136,233 pairs | #1 is the Staines reservoirs pair, the most dissimilar pair in the UK. #2 is open water next to a business park; it looks like Cardiff Bay. #3 isn't a reservoir: it's a long strip of fenland fields, but in the 2024 embeddings it reads as water. My guess is a flood-storage washland such as the Ouse Washes, which would be under water in winter. That makes it a good story card. |

| **81 Industrial and transport** | top 0.03–0.12% | Industrial strips next to big farmed parishes. #2 has docks across from a power station and mudflats; #3 is an industrial estate in Northern Ireland against fields. |

| **50 Industrial and retail parks** | top 0.01–0.12% | #1 repeats the reservoir pair #2 (the same pair seen from the other side). #2 and #3 are retail and industrial parks right against open moorland in the Pennines, which is striking. |

| **42 Golf and leafy suburbs** | top 0.05–0.13% | #1 is a golf course with a large estate. #2 is a historic park with an avenue and lakes, probably a royal park in south-west London. #3 is a common or heath next to terraces and a stadium. More "parks" than golf. |

| **91 Woodland and heathland** | top 0.01–0.15% | Forest and heath against small housing estates; looks like Surrey/Hampshire and the Weald. All clear. |

| **90 Harbour and marina** | top 0.04–0.19% | Small seaside settlements next to huge rural parishes. The pictures are good, but the contrast is town versus countryside more than waterfront. |

| **87 Ports and coastal towns** | #123, #220, #232 | Small harbour towns against farmland, coast, or island moorland and lochs (#3 is in Shetland). Clouds show in #1 and #2. |

| **93 Coastal fringe** | top 0.10–0.41% | Saltmarsh, dunes and a spit next to housing. #3 is a dune area against a seafront town centre. The most "map-like" set. |

| **88 Central mixed use** | top 0.75–2.6% | Central London blocks against the big parks: looks like Hyde Park, Regent's Park and a riverside park. The best-looking set, even though the distances are the lowest. |

**Problems:**

- The same pair can appear under two entities. The reservoir/business-park pair shows up under both 99 and 50; a pair should go to only one entity.

- The Esri imagery shows clouds in a few cards (81 #3, 87 #1 and #2).

- Ranks are against all pairs in the UK, so the 88 cards look "weak" by number but strong visually.

- 99 #1 and #3 (Staines; the fenland washland)

- 50 #2 (retail park against moorland)

- 42 #2 (historic park)

I'd submit two cards, with an optional third.

**1. Staines reservoirs: `E01030745` and `E01030710`, the UK's most dissimilar neighbouring pair**

- **Why it's striking:** two huge black reservoirs pressed against a tight grid of suburban housing. You read the contrast instantly.

- **What it shows:** this is the headline result. At a cosine distance of 0.538 it is #1 of all 136,233 neighbouring pairs. The same area also tops `mean_dist` and `lag_dist`, so the result holds however you measure it.

**2. Nene Washes: `E01018058` and `E01018072`, ranked #32 of 136,233**

- **Why it's striking:** it's a puzzle. In the photo both areas look like fenland fields, yet the embeddings put them among the most different pairs in the UK, and the pair landed in the reservoirs cluster.

- **What it shows:** I checked the location. It's between Peterborough and Whittlesey, which matches the Nene Washes, a flood-storage washland that sits under water for much of the winter. I haven't confirmed that against the embeddings themselves, so treat it as the likely explanation.

  - One photo can't show seasonal flooding, but an embedding that summarises the whole of 2024 can. That's exactly the case for embeddings over imagery.
  - On this card, the band chart (grey for what's shared, colour for the gap) earns its place.
- **Correction:** I called this the Ouse Washes earlier. The coordinates put it at the Nene Washes.

**Optional third: Macclesfield retail park and the moors: `E01018631` and `E01018669`**

- **Why it's striking:** a retail and industrial park on the edge of Macclesfield, with the Peak District moorland directly beside it. It's top 0.07% of pairs.

- **What it shows:** it's the cluster idea working. We asked "what's the most different thing next to an industrial park?" and got an answer you wouldn't find by browsing. It also avoids water, so the set isn't three water stories.

**Why not the others:**

- **Business-core cards:** the distances are weaker, or the pictures need explaining.

- **Central London block next to a park:** it looks lovely but is only top 0.75%.

- **Port cards:** they have cloud in the imagery.

**Before posting, re-export the chosen cards at 200 dpi into `figures/` with consistent captions:**

```{=html}
for name,x,y,place,kw in cards:

    else: kw={&quot;emb&quot;:(bands.loc[x],bands.loc[y])}
```

- **Why it's the best third card:** the set already has "obviously different" (Staines) and "the embedding sees what the photo can't" (Nene Washes). This one makes a third point: embeddings tell kinds of urban fabric apart, not just built-up versus open land.

- **Caveat:** that the gap comes from the housing form (terraces vs flats, more tree cover) is my reading; I haven't tested it. "Kensal area" comes from the coordinates (51.528, −0.210), so please check the name before posting.

**B. Hackney Marshes, east London: `E01001786` and `E01001785`. Distance 0.375, #103 of 136,233 pairs.**

- Playing fields ringed by woodland, next to a tight grid of terraces, all inside the city. The coordinates match Hackney Marshes.

- It's more striking and ranks higher, but it's the same "built-up against open land" contrast as Staines.

Whichever you choose, I'll export it at 200 dpi to `figures/final/` to replace the Macclesfield card. I can also record the final set in the notebook and the log.

::: {.reply}
You're right: to the eye they're the same kind of place. That's why I'd drop the Kensal pair as a submission card.

**What the embeddings say:**

- Neither area is an outlier. Each sits comfortably inside its own k=100 cluster: `E01004721` is in cluster 68 and `E01004722` in cluster 69, and each is about as close to its cluster centre as a typical member. Their most similar areas elsewhere are ordinary members of the same clusters.

- So this isn't small-area noise, as it partly was in Glasgow. The model consistently separates two kinds of place, and the centres of clusters 68 and 69 are 0.299 apart. That's as far apart as many pairs of housing and woodland.

**What the imagery shows:** I made sheets of 9 typical areas from each cluster, also sent. Both look like dense terraced housing. Cluster 69 is slightly more uniform Victorian terraces (94% England); cluster 68 mixes in some flats and estates, with 15% Scotland and 11% Northern Ireland. Nothing explains a gap that large.

**My best guess, which I haven't tested:**

- **Street orientation.** On the card, the orange terraces mostly run east–west and the green ones north–south.

- AlphaEarth includes radar (Sentinel-1), and radar returns from buildings depend strongly on how the streets are oriented relative to the satellite's path. This is a known effect, sometimes called the cardinal effect.

- Two identical terraced grids at right angles could look very different to the model.

- **One way to test it:** compute the dominant street direction of areas in clusters 68 and 69 from OpenStreetMap and see whether it separates them.

**For the submission:** a card whose main contrast we can't explain, and which may be a sensor artefact, is risky as a showcase. I'd use **Hackney Marshes** as the third card instead. It sits entirely within London, ranks #103 of 136,233, and the contrast is real and easy to read.

The Kensal pair would make a good follow-up: "what are embeddings actually seeing?"

If you agree, I'll export Hackney Marshes to `figures/final/` to replace Macclesfield.

````{=html}
```python
MIN_KM2 = 0.05
km2 = lsoas.area / 1e6
pair_rank = lambda d: int((pair_dist &gt; d).sum()) + 1

def top_pairs(members, n=3, min_km2=MIN_KM2):
    &quot;&quot;&quot;Top n distinct neighbouring pairs that include an area in `members`, member first, both areas &gt;= min_km2.&quot;&quot;&quot;
    p = pair_dist.reset_index()
    in_a, in_b = p.a.isin(members), p.b.isin(members)
    p = p[in_a | in_b]
    swap = ~in_a[p.index]
    p.loc[swap, [&quot;a&quot;, &quot;b&quot;]] = p.loc[swap, [&quot;b&quot;, &quot;a&quot;]].to_numpy()
    p = p[(km2[p.a].to_numpy() &gt;= min_km2) &amp; (km2[p.b].to_numpy() &gt;= min_km2)].sort_values(&quot;dist&quot;, ascending=False)
    used, picks = set(), []
    for row in p.itertuples():
        if row.a in used or row.b in used:
            continue
        picks.append(row)
        used |= {row.a, row.b}
        if len(picks) == n:
            break
    return pd.DataFrame(picks).drop(columns=&quot;Index&quot;)

entity_pairs = pd.concat({
    k: top_pairs(set(clusters.index[clusters.c100 == k])) for k in ENTITIES if k != 95
}, names=[&quot;c100&quot;, &quot;i&quot;]).reset_index()
````

# #30DayMapChallenge — Day 10: neighbours, near and far

This notebook builds the final submission from start to end. Every small area in the UK (LSOAs in England and Wales, Data Zones in Scotland, Super Data Zones in Northern Ireland) has an AlphaEarth embedding for 2024: 64 numbers summarising a year of satellite observations. We compare every pair of neighbouring areas and turn three of them into Polaroid cards:

1. **The most different neighbours** in the UK.
2. **The most similar neighbours.**
3. **The most similar urban neighbours.**

The exploration behind these choices lives in `gdsl30dmc.ipynb` and `gdsl30dmc_clusters.ipynb`; this notebook depends only on the shared module `gdsl30dmc_tools.py` (data loading, contiguity and the Polaroid card template).
@@markdown
## Setup

Libraries for the whole pipeline. The shared module also registers the card fonts: Figtree for the caption and Special Elite, a typewriter face, for the haiku.

import pandas as pd

import gdsl30dmc_tools as tools
EOF

## Areas and their neighbours

We read the 2024 areas with their mean embeddings and connect every pair of areas whose polygons touch or overlap (fuzzy contiguity: queen contiguity plus the England–Scotland border, where the two nations&#x27; polygons overlap). Twelve island areas have no neighbours, so we drop them.
@@code
%%time
YEAR = 2024
areas = tools.load_areas(YEAR)
g = tools.contiguity(areas)
areas, g = tools.drop_isolates(areas, g)
print(f&quot;{len(areas):,} areas | {g.n_edges // 2:,} neighbouring pairs&quot;)
@@markdown
## How different is each pair of neighbours?

For every neighbouring pair we compute the cosine distance between their embeddings: 0 means the two areas look the same to the model, and larger values mean more different. We compute it from scratch here (`cache=None`) rather than reading the copy cached by the exploration notebooks. Each pair appears once, with its two codes in alphabetical order.
@@code
dist = tools.pair_distances(areas, g, cache=None)
km2 = areas.area / 1e6
pairs = dist.reset_index().assign(km2_a=lambda d: km2[d.a].to_numpy(), km2_b=lambda d: km2[d.b].to_numpy())
pairs.dist.describe().round(4)
EOF

@@markdown
## Picking the three pairs

- **Most different:** the pair with the largest distance.
- **Most similar:** the pair with the smallest distance.
- **Most similar urban:** the smallest distance among pairs where both areas cover between 0.05 and 1 km². Areas are drawn to hold similar numbers of people, so small areas are urban. The lower bound leaves out tiny areas, whose average embedding rests on only a few hundred 10 m pixels and is less reliable.

On each card, the larger of the two areas is outlined in orange and the other in green.
@@code
URBAN_KM2 = (0.05, 1.0)
urban = pairs.km2_a.between(*URBAN_KM2) &amp; pairs.km2_b.between(*URBAN_KM2)

picks = pd.DataFrame({
    &quot;most_different&quot;: pairs.loc[pairs.dist.idxmax()],
    &quot;most_similar&quot;: pairs.loc[pairs.dist.idxmin()],
    &quot;most_similar_urban&quot;: pairs[urban].loc[pairs[urban].dist.idxmin()],
}).T
swap = picks.km2_b &gt; picks.km2_a  # larger area first, so it is drawn in orange
picks.loc[swap, [&quot;a&quot;, &quot;b&quot;, &quot;km2_a&quot;, &quot;km2_b&quot;]] = picks.loc[swap, [&quot;b&quot;, &quot;a&quot;, &quot;km2_b&quot;, &quot;km2_a&quot;]].to_numpy()
picks[&quot;rank_different&quot;] = [int((dist &gt; d).sum()) + 1 for d in picks.dist]
picks[&quot;rank_similar&quot;] = [int((dist &lt; d).sum()) + 1 for d in picks.dist]
picks
EOF

````{=html}
@@markdown
## Captions

Each card carries a place name, read off the areas&#x27; location, and a haiku in place of statistics. The `expect` codes guard the captions: if the data or the rules ever change and a different pair is picked, the notebook stops instead of printing the wrong poem on a new picture.
@@code
N = len(dist)
CAPTIONS = {
    &quot;most_different&quot;: dict(
        expect={&quot;E01030745&quot;, &quot;E01030710&quot;}, place=&quot;Staines reservoirs, Surrey&quot;,
        rank=lambda r: f&quot;#1 most different of {N:,}&quot;,
        haiku=&quot;Still black reservoir —\nthe next street hangs out washing.\nNothing more apart.&quot;),
    &quot;most_similar&quot;: dict(
        expect={&quot;N20000681&quot;, &quot;N20000689&quot;}, place=&quot;Farmland, County Armagh&quot;,
        rank=lambda r: f&quot;#1 most similar of {N:,}&quot;,
        haiku=&quot;Green field, hedge, green field.\nA map line says they are two;\nthe land knows just one.&quot;),
    &quot;most_similar_urban&quot;: dict(
        expect={&quot;E01003685&quot;, &quot;E01003730&quot;}, place=&quot;Ilford, east London&quot;,
        rank=lambda r: f&quot;most similar urban pair (#{r.rank_similar} of {N:,})&quot;,
        haiku=&quot;Same bay window, same\nchimney pots, same Tuesday bins.\nTwo codes, one long street.&quot;),
}
for kind, r in picks.iterrows():
    assert {r.a, r.b} == CAPTIONS[kind][&quot;expect&quot;], f&quot;{kind}: picked {r.a}–{r.b}, captions were written for another pair&quot;
@@markdown
## The cards

Each card is a Polaroid: Esri satellite imagery washed out except over the two areas, the pair&#x27;s codes as the title, the place, distance and rank underneath, the haiku in a typewriter face, and a UK locator. Cards are saved at 200 dpi to `figures/submission/`.
@@code
%%time
uk_outline = tools.uk_outline(areas)
out_dir = tools.FIG_DIR / &quot;submission&quot;
for i, (kind, r) in enumerate(picks.iterrows(), 1):
    cap = CAPTIONS[kind]
    d = f&quot;{r.dist:.3f}&quot; if r.dist &gt;= 0.01 else f&quot;{r.dist:.4f}&quot;
    subtitle = f&quot;{cap[&#x27;place&#x27;]}  ·  distance {d}  ·  {cap[&#x27;rank&#x27;](r)}&quot;
    fig = tools.pair_card(areas, r.a, r.b, subtitle, uk_outline, haiku=cap[&quot;haiku&quot;])
    print(tools.export_card(fig, f&quot;{i}_{kind}&quot;, fig_dir=out_dir).relative_to(tools.ROOT))
````

#30DayMapChallenge, day 10: prompting only.

Every small area in the UK (46,832 of them) has a 2024 AlphaEarth embedding, made available through Imago: 64 numbers that sum up a year of satellite observations. Compare each area with the ones it touches and you get 136,233 pairs of neighbours, ranked from most different to most alike.

```{=html}
# #30DayMapChallenge, Submission Day 10

&gt; &quot;Prompting only&quot; - For this map, make AI work for its money and produce something
from start to finish in a chat window or on the command line.

We are going to be working towards building a submission for this day. The
idea is to create a map of the areas in the UK with the most dissimilar
neighboring LSOAs. We will measure similarity with AlphaEarth embeddings, and
areas with official LSOA polygons. 

## Data

We are going to be working with Imago&#x27;s embeddings product:

&gt; https://data.imago.ac.uk/datasets/google-satellite-embedding-v1-small-areas-2017-2024

We will start playing with 2024, but we might explore looking at change later
on.

## Similarity

In this context, we will describe similarity of two LSOAs as the distance 
between their two embedding vectors.
```

```{=html}
## Reading a card

Each card is a Polaroid of one pair of neighbouring areas. The two areas are outlined in orange and green over Esri satellite imagery, and everything else is washed out. Underneath are the areas&#x27; official codes, the place, the cosine distance between their embeddings (0 means identical; the largest in the UK is 0.538) and its rank among all pairs. The UK locator shows where the pair is. The haiku says what the numbers can&#x27;t.

The submission is three cards, but it took {{&lt; var n_prompts &gt;}} prompts over {{&lt; var n_days &gt;}} days to get there. This is the route, chapter by chapter. Each chapter quotes the prompts that turned the corner: the typed notes are the human&#x27;s words, unedited, and their numbers link to the exact spot in the [transcript](transcript.qmd). The images are what Claude looked at along the way, most of which never made it into a notebook.

## 1 · The brief

The project started from a short brief, `SPEC.md`: map the UK&#x27;s most dissimilar neighbouring small areas, measuring similarity with AlphaEarth embeddings from [Imago](https://data.imago.ac.uk/datasets/google-satellite-embedding-v1-small-areas-2017-2024), using geopandas and PySAL&#x27;s new `Graph`, and keeping a log of explorations.

{{&lt; include _generated/prompt-1.md &gt;}}

## 2 · Who touches whom

Before comparing neighbours, we need to know who the neighbours are. Queen contiguity (areas sharing at least a corner) across all four nations gave a graph with one surprise: no links at all across the England–Scotland border, because the two nations&#x27; polygons overlap rather than touch. Fuzzy contiguity, which also counts overlaps, fixed that with 21 extra links. Twelve island areas had no neighbours at all and were dropped.

{{&lt; include _generated/prompt-2.md &gt;}}
{{&lt; include _generated/prompt-6.md &gt;}}

::: {.polaroid .tilt-l}
![](conversation/img/001.jpg)
[The twelve areas with no neighbours, all of them Scottish islands.]{.caption}
:::

## 3 · Measuring difference

Each area&#x27;s embedding is a 64-number vector; the difference between two neighbours is the cosine distance between their vectors, computed for all 136,233 neighbouring pairs. The human pushed for splitting the work into 16 chunks, one per core, which (after a detour about threads versus processes and memory layout) made it fast.

{{&lt; include _generated/prompt-11.md &gt;}}
{{&lt; include _generated/prompt-13.md &gt;}}

We also scored each area against its whole neighbourhood, in two ways: the average distance to each neighbour (`mean_dist`), and the distance to the average neighbour (`lag_dist`).

{{&lt; include _generated/prompt-18.md &gt;}}

## 4 · Finding a look

The first maps were plain: satellite imagery with the area and its neighbours outlined. Then came a long stretch of iteration on the look, which became the Polaroid card used on every map since.
```

````{=html}
title: &quot;Notebooks&quot;

All the analysis lives in three Jupyter notebooks and one shared Python module. Claude wrote and ran them, cell by cell, through the [`nb`](https://github.com/jupyter-ai-contrib/nb-cli) command-line tool ({{&lt; var n_nb &gt;}} `nb` commands in the [transcript](transcript.qmd)). They are shown here with the outputs saved when they were last run; the site doesn&#x27;t re-run them.

[1 · Neighbours and distances](gdsl30dmc.ipynb) (`gdsl30dmc.ipynb`)
: Reads the 2024 areas and embeddings, builds the neighbour graph (fuzzy contiguity, fixing the England–Scotland border), drops the 12 islands, computes the cosine distance for every neighbouring pair in parallel, scores each area against its neighbourhood (`mean_dist`, `lag_dist`), and makes the first Polaroid cards of the most different areas and pairs.

[2 · Clusters and entities](gdsl30dmc_clusters.ipynb) (`gdsl30dmc_clusters.ipynb`)
: Clusters the embeddings with k-means at k=20 and k=100, labels them with contact sheets, then searches for contrasts by type: business cores, reservoirs, industrial estates, golf courses, woodland, harbours. Also where the histogram and embedding band charts were developed, and where the west London housing puzzle is written up.

[3 · The submission, end to end](gdsl30dmc_submission.ipynb) (`gdsl30dmc_submission.ipynb`)
: The short, standalone pipeline behind the three cards: data → neighbours → distances → three pairs picked by rule → captions and haiku → cards. Start here if you want to reproduce the submission.

`gdsl30dmc_tools.py`
: The shared module: data loading, contiguity, distance caches, and the Polaroid card template (`polaroid`, `pair_card`, `area_card`) with its options (histogram, embedding band chart, haiku).
````

```{=html}
**#30DayMapChallenge · Day 10 · Prompting only**

The UK&#x27;s most different and most alike neighbouring small areas, seen through [AlphaEarth](https://deepmind.google/discover/blog/alphaearth-foundations-helps-map-our-planet-in-unprecedented-detail/) satellite embeddings, presented as three Polaroid cards. Everything here (the analysis, the maps, the haiku and the website) was made by prompting [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code). The website tells the story and includes the full conversation.

![The three submission cards](images/submission/1_most_different.jpg)

## What&#x27;s in the repository

| Path | What it is |
|---|---|
| `index.qmd`, `backstory.qmd`, `prompts.qmd`, `transcript.qmd`, `notebooks.qmd`, `log.qmd` | The website&#x27;s pages ([Quarto](https://quarto.org)) |
| `_quarto.yml`, `site/theme.scss` | Site configuration and the Polaroid theme |
| `docs/` | **The built website**, which GitHub Pages serves. Rebuilt by `quarto render` |
| `gdsl30dmc_submission.ipynb` | The submission, start to end: data → neighbours → distances → three pairs → cards |
| `gdsl30dmc.ipynb`, `gdsl30dmc_clusters.ipynb` | The exploration that led there |

| `data/` | **Not included.** See below |

## Publish the website on GitHub Pages

The site is already built in `docs/`, so publishing needs no tools:

1. Push this folder to a GitHub repository (e.g. `git init`, `git add .`, `git commit -m &quot;Day 10&quot;`, then push).
2. On GitHub, open the repository&#x27;s **Settings → Pages**.
3. Under **Build and deployment**, set **Source** to *Deploy from a branch*, choose your branch (`main`) and the **`/docs`** folder, and **Save**.
4. After a minute or two the site is live at `https://&lt;your-user&gt;.github.io/&lt;repository&gt;/`.

`docs/.nojekyll` tells GitHub not to process the files with Jekyll; it&#x27;s recreated on every render, so leave it there.
```

The Quarto site is built and ready to publish from `docs/`. I tested it in a clean copy containing only the files that will go in the repo, with no data: it builds fully in about 15 seconds. In a headless browser every page loaded with no broken links or errors. I've sent screenshots of the home page, a backstory chapter and the transcript.

**What's on the site**

- **The submission (home page):** the three cards first, then a short "reading a card", the LinkedIn post, a few numbers (63 prompts, about 2,000 words typed, 296 tool calls, 84 images Claude looked at) and a way into the rest.

- **Backstory:** 11 short chapters, from the brief to this site, showing the dead ends and the images Claude looked at along the way. Most of those images never made it into a notebook: the first raw maps, the 15-style grid, the cluster sheets, the west London puzzle.

- **The prompts:** every message you typed, in order and unedited, typos included. On a prompting-only day that's effectively the source code.

- **Transcript:** the whole conversation, grouped by day.

  - Claude's replies, with tool calls folded away as expandable steps.
  - Every image Claude viewed or sent you.
  - The context summary, shown where it happened.
- **Notebooks:** the three notebooks with their saved outputs, plus an introduction page.

- **Log:** `LOG.md`.

**How the conversation runs through the site**

- Your prompts appear as typed notes with a strip of tape, in the same typewriter face as the haiku.

- They're quoted in the backstory where each turn happened.

- Every note's number links to that moment in the transcript.

- The counts on the home page come from the transcript itself, so they stay correct if you re-export it.

**Styling:** prints on a light table. The cards are slightly tilted, with shadows. Other images get a Polaroid frame with a typed caption. It uses the Imago colours and Figtree, and works at phone width.

**What I added to the folder**

- `README.md`: publishing, rebuilding, re-running the analysis and getting the data.

- `requirements.txt` and `.gitignore`.

- `fonts/README.md` with the font licences.

- `scripts/`, three helpers:

  - `export_conversation.py` turns the Claude Code session file into `conversation/`.
  - `build_site.py` builds the web images, transcript and prompt pages, and runs automatically before every render.
  - `post_render.py` adds the file GitHub Pages needs.

**Data**

- `data/` is git-ignored, and the README says where to download the 2024 GeoPackage and what to name it.

- Full-resolution figures are ignored too, except the three submission cards. The site uses smaller web copies, which are committed.

- The repo comes to about 108 MB, mostly images, so it can be pushed as is.

**Publishing on GitHub Pages**

1. Push the folder to a GitHub repository.

2. Go to **Settings → Pages → Build and deployment**.

3. Set **Source** to *Deploy from a branch*, choose `main` and the **`/docs`** folder, and save.

4. After a minute or two the site is live at `https://<user>.github.io/<repo>/`.

To change anything later, run `quarto render`, which needs only Quarto and Pillow, then commit `docs/`.

**Before you make it public**

- **The transcript is the conversation as it happened**, apart from four things removed:

  - your email address;
  - machine paths;
  - Claude's internal reasoning;
  - the instructions the tool injects.

  It includes your typos and passing remarks. Skim **The prompts** page first.
- **The transcript stops partway through building this site.** To include the end of the conversation, re-run the export command in the README, then `quarto render`.

- **No log entry yet** for the website. I can add one if you want.
